drills.los_text: evaluate strategies for managing a single liability

questions.stem: Immunization is best described as a process that seeks to:

options.A: Minimize the variance in a portfolio's realized return over a known time horizon.
options.B: Eliminate credit risk by holding only government-guaranteed securities.
options.C: Maximize expected return without regard to the timing of obligations.

rationales.A: Immunization is the process of structuring and managing a fixed-income bond portfolio to minimize the variance in the realized rate of return over a known time horizon. That variance arises from the volatility of future interest rates. Default risk is neglected in this framework because the portfolio bonds are assumed to have default probabilities that approach zero, so the risk being managed is interest rate risk: the price risk on the bonds and the reinvestment risk on their coupons, which offset one another when the horizon is matched to the portfolio's Macaulay duration.
rationales.B: The technique addresses interest rate risk over a known horizon rather than the elimination of credit risk. Default risk is set aside in the immunization framework precisely because the portfolio bonds are assumed to have default probabilities approaching zero; restricting holdings to government-guaranteed securities would therefore do nothing to minimize the variance of the realized rate of return over the horizon, which is what immunization seeks to do.
rationales.C: Immunization targets an obligation due on a known date and minimizes the variance of the realized rate of return to that date; maximizing expected return is not the objective. A portfolio assembled without regard to the timing of the obligation would leave the price effect and the coupon reinvestment effect unmatched at the horizon, so the realized return would vary with future interest rates.

questions.stem: The most obvious way to immunize the interest rate risk on a single liability is most likely to:

options.A: Buy a zero-coupon bond maturing on the obligation's due date.
options.B: Buy a coupon-bearing bond maturing on the obligation's due date.
options.C: Hold a floating-rate note to the obligation's due date.

rationales.A: The most obvious way to immunize the interest rate risk on a single liability is to buy a zero-coupon bond that matures on the obligation's due date, with a face value that matches the liability amount. There is no cash flow reinvestment risk, because there are no coupon payments to reinvest, and there is no price risk, because the bond is held to maturity; any interest rate volatility over the bond's lifetime is therefore irrelevant to the asset's ability to pay off the liability. The practical problem is that in many financial markets zero-coupon bonds are not available. Nevertheless, the perfect immunization a zero-coupon bond provides sets the standard against which the performance of immunizing strategies that use coupon-bearing bonds is measured.
rationales.B: A coupon bond maturing on the due date still carries cash flow reinvestment risk on its interim coupons. The rates at which those coupons can be reinvested are unknown today, so the value accumulated by the due date varies with future interest rates and, unlike a zero-coupon bond, the position cannot guarantee the amount needed to pay the liability.
rationales.C: A floating-rate note's coupon resets keep its price close to par, but each reset changes the cash flows received, so the terminal accumulated value remains uncertain as rates change. Price risk is stabilized at the cost of coupon and reinvestment uncertainty, and the position therefore cannot lock in the amount required on the obligation's due date.

questions.stem: For a coupon bond held through a one-time shift in the yield curve, the point in time at which the price effect and the coupon reinvestment effect cancel each other out is most likely the bond's:

options.A: Maturity date.
options.B: Modified duration.
options.C: Macaulay duration.

rationales.A: At the maturity date there is no remaining price effect to offset, because the price has been pulled to par, while the reinvestment effect on the coupons already received is fully realized. The two effects offset earlier, at the Macaulay duration point, not at maturity. Maturity is the offset point only for a zero-coupon bond, whose Macaulay duration equals its maturity.
rationales.B: The offset occurs at the Macaulay duration, not the modified duration. Modified duration equals Macaulay duration divided by one plus the periodic yield; it measures price sensitivity and is shorter than the point in time at which the two effects cancel, so an investment horizon matched to it would leave the price and coupon reinvestment effects unbalanced.
rationales.C: Assume the bond is currently priced at par value and that an instantaneous, one-time upward parallel shift occurs in the yield curve. The bond's value falls, and that drop is estimated by the money duration of the bond, which is the modified duration statistic multiplied by the price. Subsequently the bond price is pulled to par as the maturity date nears. But another factor is at work: assuming interest rates remain higher, the future value of the reinvested coupon payments goes up. At some point in time the two effects, the price effect and the coupon reinvestment effect, cancel each other out, and that point turns out to be the bond's Macaulay duration (for a zero-coupon bond, its Macaulay duration is its maturity). Therefore an investor having an investment horizon equal to the bond's Macaulay duration is effectively protected, or immunized, from interest rate risk, in that the price and coupon reinvestment effects offset for either higher or lower rates.

questions.stem: A bond's money duration is most likely equal to its:

options.A: Modified duration divided by price.
options.B: Macaulay duration multiplied by price.
options.C: Modified duration multiplied by price.

rationales.A: This inverts the relationship: money, or dollar, duration multiplies modified duration by price rather than dividing by it. Dividing would make the measure smaller as the position gets larger, which is the opposite of how a money measure of interest rate risk behaves.
rationales.B: This substitutes Macaulay duration for modified duration. Money duration uses the modified duration statistic, which equals Macaulay duration divided by one plus the periodic yield; using Macaulay duration instead would overstate the estimated change in the bond's value for a given rate shift.
rationales.C: Money duration, also known as dollar duration, is the bond's modified duration statistic multiplied by the price, or, at the portfolio level, the portfolio modified duration multiplied by the market value. The drop in a bond's value from a rate shift is estimated by its money duration. To keep the numbers manageable, the basis point value (BPV) measure is often used: it is the money duration multiplied by 1 bp, or 0.0001, so a money duration of EUR1,178,237,935 gives a BPV of EUR117,824. A closely related risk measure is the present value of a basis point (PVBP), also called the PV01 (present value of an '01', meaning 1 bp) and, in North America, the DV01 (dollar value of an '01').

questions.stem: A portfolio of coupon-bearing bonds is assembled to immunize a single EUR 250 million liability due in six years. The essential property the portfolio must exhibit is most likely:

options.A: A portfolio Macaulay duration of six years.
options.B: A weighted average maturity of six years.
options.C: A portfolio modified duration of six years.

rationales.A: Immunizing a single liability with coupon-bearing bonds requires matching the portfolio's Macaulay duration to the horizon date, with a market value at least equal to the present value of the liability and with the dispersion of cash flows, and hence convexity, minimized. At the Macaulay duration point the price effect and the coupon reinvestment effect offset, which locks in the cash flow yield. For a EUR 250 million liability due 15 February 2027, a six-year horizon from 15 February 2021, a three-bond portfolio with a market value of EUR 200,052,250 and a cash flow yield of 3.7608% is immunized by setting its Macaulay duration equal to that six-year horizon.
rationales.B: Matching the weighted average maturity of the component bonds does not align the timing of the portfolio's cash flows with the horizon, because maturity ignores the size and timing of the interim coupons. It is the Macaulay duration, the money-weighted average time to receipt of the portfolio's cash flows, that must be matched to the six-year investment horizon.
rationales.C: It is the Macaulay duration, not the modified duration, that is set equal to the horizon. Modified duration equals Macaulay duration divided by one plus the periodic yield, so matching modified duration to six years would leave the Macaulay duration above target and the horizon mismatched.

questions.stem: The cash flow yield on a portfolio used to immunize a liability is best described as:

options.A: The market-value-weighted average of the bonds' yields to maturity.
options.B: The realized holding period return under any reinvestment rate.
options.C: The internal rate of return on the portfolio's cash flows.

rationales.A: The cash flow yield is the internal rate of return on the portfolio's aggregate cash flows, and it generally differs from the weighted average of the component bonds' yields to maturity. Treating the two as equivalent is exactly the interpretation the reading warns against, because averaging yields ignores the timing and size of the pooled cash flows from which the internal rate of return is computed.
rationales.B: The realized holding period return matches the cash flow yield only if the coupon payments are reinvested at that same yield and the bonds are held to maturity or sold at a point on the constant-yield price trajectory. If coupons are reinvested at other rates, the realized return departs from the cash flow yield, which is why reinvestment risk remains the central concern in immunization.
rationales.C: The cash flow yield is the internal rate of return on the portfolio's cash flows, and the holding period rate of return, also called the horizon yield, equals it. For a portfolio with an original market value of 200,052,250 that produces a total of 250,167,000 over six years, the semiannual solution to 200,052,250 = 250,167,000 / (1 + ROR/2)^12 is ROR = 0.037608, or 3.7608%, the same figure as the cash flow yield. This equivalence is the multi-bond version of the well-known result for a single bond: the realized rate of return matches the yield to maturity only if coupon payments are reinvested at that same yield and if the bond is held to maturity or sold at a point on the constant-yield price trajectory.

questions.stem: In the expression for an immunized portfolio's convexity, the numerator is most likely:

options.A: Macaulay duration squared, less Macaulay duration, plus dispersion.
options.B: Macaulay duration squared, plus Macaulay duration, less dispersion.
options.C: Macaulay duration squared, plus Macaulay duration, plus dispersion.

rationales.A: This flips the sign on the linear Macaulay duration term. Immunized portfolio convexity = (MacDur² + MacDur + Dispersion) / (1 + Cash flow yield)², so the Macaulay duration term is added, not subtracted; subtracting it would understate convexity and therefore understate the structural risk the statistic is meant to measure.
rationales.B: Dispersion is added in the numerator, so subtracting it misstates the structural-risk relationship. In semiannual periods, a portfolio with a Macaulay duration of 12.0008, dispersion of 33.0378 and a cash flow yield of 1.8804% has convexity (12.0008² + 12.0008 + 33.0378) / (1.018804)² = 182.1437; subtracting dispersion would give a materially lower figure and would wrongly imply that more widely dispersed cash flows reduce the risk to the immunization strategy.
rationales.C: Immunized portfolio convexity = (MacDur² + MacDur + Dispersion) / (1 + Cash flow yield)². In terms of semiannual periods, for a portfolio whose Macaulay duration is 12.0008, dispersion is 33.0378 and cash flow yield is 1.8804%, immunized portfolio convexity = (12.0008² + 12.0008 + 33.0378) / (1.018804)² = 182.1437. The portfolio dispersion and convexity statistics are used to assess the structural risk to the interest rate immunization strategy, and that structural risk arises from the potential for shifts and twists to the yield curve.

questions.stem: A parallel, or shape-preserving, shift in the yield curve, in which all yields change by the same amount in the same direction, is most likely:

options.A: Unrelated to the success of immunization.
options.B: Necessary for immunization to succeed.
options.C: Sufficient but not necessary for immunization to succeed.

rationales.A: Curve movements are precisely the risk that immunization manages, so they bear directly on whether the portfolio achieves its target return; the question at issue is which movements guarantee success, not whether movements matter. Dispersion and convexity are measured for the sole purpose of assessing exposure to shifts and twists in the curve.
rationales.B: Parallel, or shape-preserving, shifts are sufficient but not necessary. If the change in the portfolio's cash flow yield is the same as the change on the zero-coupon bond being replicated, immunization can be achieved even with a non-parallel shift to the yield curve, so immunization does not always fail when the shift is non-parallel.
rationales.C: A sufficient, but not necessary, condition for immunization is a parallel, or shape-preserving, shift whereby all yields change by the same amount in the same direction. If the change in the cash flow yield is the same as that on the zero-coupon bond being replicated, immunization can be achieved even with a non-parallel shift to the yield curve. That is why structural risk, the exposure to shifts and twists in the curve, is managed by minimizing dispersion and convexity rather than by assuming parallel shifts.

questions.stem: Structural risk to an interest rate immunization strategy most likely:

options.A: Is a form of default risk on the bonds held.
options.B: Is the risk of shifts and twists in the yield curve.
options.C: Is minimized by holding the highest available convexity.

rationales.A: Structural risk is an interest rate phenomenon, the potential for non-parallel shifts and twists in the yield curve, not a credit phenomenon. Default risk is a separate consideration in selecting portfolio holdings, and the immunization framework sets it aside by assuming the portfolio bonds have default probabilities that approach zero.
rationales.B: Structural risk arises from the potential for shifts and twists to the yield curve, and the portfolio dispersion and convexity statistics are used to assess it. The risk is minimized by selecting the portfolio with the lower convexity, and hence the lower dispersion of cash flows, because cash flows clustered close to the horizon date behave more like the single zero-coupon bond the strategy is replicating.
rationales.C: Structural risk is minimized by selecting the portfolio with the lower convexity, and the lower dispersion of cash flows, not the highest convexity available. If a portfolio's convexity is high, its cash flow dispersion is high, which means greater risk to the immunization from non-parallel shifts and twists in the yield curve.

questions.stem: A bond portfolio immunizing a single liability is most likely to require rebalancing:

options.A: Never, once duration is matched at inception.
options.B: Only when a bond matures or leaves the portfolio.
options.C: As time passes and bond yields change.

rationales.A: Duration drifts as time passes and yields change, because the Macaulay duration of the bonds does not decline in lockstep with the remaining horizon. The match therefore degrades even when the bonds are simply held to the horizon date, and the portfolio must be rebalanced by buying and selling bonds or by using interest rate derivatives such as futures contracts and interest rate swaps.
rationales.B: Yield changes themselves alter the bonds' durations, so the portfolio can drift away from its duration target with no bond maturing or otherwise leaving the portfolio. Rebalancing is driven by the duration mismatch however that mismatch arises, including the simple passage of time.
rationales.C: In the case of a single liability, immunization is achieved by matching the Macaulay duration of the bond portfolio to the horizon date. As time passes and bond yields change, the duration of the bonds changes and the portfolio needs to be rebalanced. This rebalancing can be accomplished by buying and selling bonds or by using interest rate derivatives, such as futures contracts and interest rate swaps.

questions.stem: An immunization strategy is most likely designed to lock in the portfolio's:

options.A: weighted average yield to maturity.
options.B: coupon income alone.
options.C: cash flow yield.

rationales.A: This interpretation is explicitly rejected. The immunization target is the cash flow yield on the portfolio — the internal rate of return on the portfolio's cash flows — and that internal rate of return generally differs from the weighted average of the yields to maturity on the individual bonds that constitute the portfolio. The weighted average of component yields ignores the timing and size of the aggregate cash flow stream, which is exactly what the internal rate of return captures.
rationales.B: Immunization locks in a total return, not an income stream. That total return is the internal rate of return on all of the portfolio's cash flows — coupon receipts, the reinvestment of those coupons, and the price change on the bonds held — so it is not the current coupon income considered independently of the rates at which coupons are reinvested. The whole point of the strategy is that reinvestment risk and price risk offset one another, which only has meaning for a measure that includes both.
rationales.C: An immunization strategy aims to lock in the cash flow yield on the portfolio, which is the internal rate of return on the portfolio's cash flows. It is not the weighted average of the yields to maturity on the bonds that constitute the portfolio, and it is not the coupon income stream taken on its own: the locked-in figure is a total return that embeds coupon reinvestment and price change over the horizon.

drills.los_text: compare strategies for a single liability and for multiple liabilities, including alternative means of implementation

questions.stem: The principle of interest rate immunization is most likely:

options.A: applicable to multiple liabilities only by matching Macaulay duration to each due date.
options.B: applicable to multiple liabilities as well as to a single liability.
options.C: applicable only to a single liability.

rationales.A: Multiple-liability immunization matches aggregate money duration — the basis point value (BPV) of the asset portfolio against the BPV of the liability portfolio — rather than matching Macaulay duration separately to each payment date. Matching a duration to every individual due date would amount to cash flow matching, a different strategy. In the single-liability case the prescription is to match the portfolio's Macaulay duration to the investment horizon while the initial investment matches or exceeds the present value of the liability; combining those two conditions is what produces the money duration match that carries over to a portfolio of liabilities.
rationales.B: The principle of interest rate immunization applies to multiple liabilities in addition to a single liability. In the single-liability case, the strategy is to match the portfolio's Macaulay duration with the investment horizon, and the initial investment needs to match or exceed the present value of the liability; combined, these two conditions prescribe that the money duration of the immunizing portfolio match the money duration of the debt liabilities. With multiple liabilities, matching money durations is the useful formulation because the market values and cash flow yields of the assets and the liabilities are not necessarily equal. Unlike the single-liability case, where the asset portfolio's modified duration (money duration) must be slightly greater than that of the liability, immunization against multiple liabilities requires that the asset portfolio's money duration (BPV) match that of the liabilities; the match may be slightly above or slightly below, provided it is the closest available to the liability BPV.
rationales.C: The immunization principle is not confined to a single liability. It extends explicitly to a portfolio of debt liabilities by matching the money duration of the assets to the money duration of the liabilities — that is, by matching basis point values — together with the conditions that the market value of the assets be at least that of the liabilities and that the dispersion of cash flows and convexity of the assets exceed those of the liabilities.

questions.stem: Immunizing a portfolio of multiple liabilities, in terms of market value, basis point value (BPV), and convexity, most likely requires:

options.A: assets at or above liabilities in market value, asset BPV above liability BPV, and greater asset convexity.
options.B: assets at or above liabilities in market value, asset BPV equal to liability BPV, and greater asset convexity.
options.C: assets equal to liabilities in market value, asset BPV equal to liability BPV, and lower asset convexity.

rationales.A: The second condition is an equality, not an inequality: the asset basis point value must equal the liability BPV. Deliberately setting asset BPV above liability BPV leaves the assets more rate-sensitive than the liabilities, so the surplus rises when rates fall and falls when rates rise. That is a directional bet on the level of interest rates, not immunization, which is meant to leave the surplus insensitive to a parallel shift. The three conditions are that the market value of assets is greater than or equal to the market value of the liabilities, that the asset BPV equals the liability BPV, and that the dispersion of cash flows and convexity of the assets are greater than those of the liabilities.
rationales.B: The conditions to immunize multiple liabilities are that (1) the market value of the assets is greater than or equal to the market value of the liabilities, (2) the asset basis point value (BPV) equals the liability BPV, and (3) the dispersion of cash flows and the convexity of the assets are greater than those of the liabilities. The first condition establishes the funded position; the second neutralizes the first-order effect of a parallel shift in rates, because equal money durations mean assets and liabilities change in value by the same currency amount per basis point; the third protects against non-parallel movements, since the asset portfolio must respond to a steepening or flattening of the curve at least as much as the liabilities do. Note that the third condition is still bounded in practice: among portfolios whose convexity exceeds that of the liabilities, the lowest such convexity is preferred, to minimize structural risk.
rationales.C: Two of the three relations are misstated. The first condition is that the market value of the assets is greater than or equal to — not exactly equal to — the market value of the liabilities; a surplus is permitted, and in practice some surplus is what makes the strategy robust. The third condition runs the other way as well: the dispersion of cash flows and the convexity of the assets must be greater than, not less than, those of the liabilities, so that the asset portfolio keeps pace with the liabilities when the yield curve twists rather than shifts in parallel. Asset convexity below liability convexity leaves the position exposed to exactly those non-parallel movements.

questions.stem: The approaches available for managing a portfolio of multiple debt liabilities are most likely:

options.A: duration matching, derivatives overlay, and purely passive contingent immunization.
options.B: duration matching, derivatives overlay, and contingent immunization.
options.C: cash flow matching, laddering, and barbelling.

rationales.A: Contingent immunization is indeed one of the three approaches, but it is misdescribed here. It is not purely passive: it is a hybrid passive-active strategy in which the asset manager may pursue active investment strategies, as if operating under a total return mandate, as long as the surplus remains above a designated threshold. Only if the actively managed assets perform poorly and the surplus evaporates does the mandate revert to the purely passive strategy of building a duration-matching portfolio and then managing it to remain on duration target.
rationales.B: The three approaches are duration matching, which extends the ideas developed for a single liability to a portfolio of debt liabilities; a derivatives overlay, in particular the use of futures contracts on government bonds within the immunization strategy to close a money duration gap without trading the underlying bonds; and contingent immunization, which allows active bond portfolio management as long as the surplus is above a designated threshold. The three differ in how the money duration match is achieved and in how much discretion the manager retains, but all three are organized around matching the money duration of assets to that of the liabilities.
rationales.C: Laddering and barbelling are portfolio maturity structures — descriptions of how cash flows are distributed across the curve — rather than approaches to managing a portfolio of debt liabilities, and cash flow matching is a separate liability-driven technique rather than one of these three alternatives. The three approaches are duration matching, a derivatives overlay using futures on government bonds, and contingent immunization.

questions.stem: The number of futures contracts needed to close the money duration gap between a portfolio's assets and liabilities, stated in basis point value (BPV) terms, is most likely:

options.A: the asset BPV minus the liability BPV, divided by the futures BPV.
options.B: the liability BPV minus the asset BPV, multiplied by the futures BPV.
options.C: the liability BPV minus the asset BPV, divided by the futures BPV.

rationales.A: The numerator is reversed. The gap to be closed is the liability portfolio BPV minus the asset portfolio BPV, because the overlay exists to bring the money duration of the assets up to (or down to) that of the liabilities. Reversing the subtraction reverses the sign of the result and therefore the direction of the trade: the manager would sell futures when the money duration of the assets needs to be raised, and buy when it needs to be reduced, widening the gap instead of closing it.
rationales.B: The BPV gap is divided by the futures BPV per contract, not multiplied by it. Division is what converts a money duration shortfall, expressed as a currency amount per basis point for the whole portfolio, into a count of contracts, since the futures BPV is the currency amount per basis point delivered by one contract. Multiplying the two produces a quantity with no interpretation as a number of contracts, and it scales the answer in the wrong direction — a more rate-sensitive contract would appear to require more contracts rather than fewer.
rationales.C: The required number of futures contracts is the liability portfolio BPV minus the asset portfolio BPV, divided by the futures BPV. If that number is positive, the asset manager buys, or goes long, the required number of contracts, which raises the money duration of the assets to match that of the liabilities. If the number is negative, the asset manager sells, or goes short, futures contracts to reduce the money duration of the assets. In practice the futures BPV itself is estimated with a common approximation: the BPV of the cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) security divided by the conversion factor for that CTD security.

questions.stem: A liability portfolio has a basis point value (BPV) of 117,824 and the corresponding asset portfolio has a BPV of 18,819. The cheapest-to-deliver security for the Treasury note futures contract used in the overlay has a BPV of 56.8727 and a conversion factor of 0.8226. The number of futures contracts required to close the money duration gap is closest to:

options.A: 2,116 contracts.
options.B: 1,432 contracts.
options.C: 1,741 contracts.

rationales.A: This multiplies the cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) BPV by the conversion factor instead of dividing by it: 56.8727 x 0.8226 = 46.7835, and (117,824 − 18,819)/46.7835 = 2,116. The futures BPV is approximated as the CTD security's BPV divided by its conversion factor, so the correct futures BPV is 56.8727/0.8226 = 69.1377. Because the conversion factor here is below 1.0000, multiplying understates the futures BPV and therefore overstates the number of contracts needed.
rationales.B: The money duration gap to be closed is 117,824 − 18,819 = 99,005. With the 6.5-year T-note as the cheapest-to-deliver security, the futures BPV is estimated as 56.8727/0.8226 = 69.1377, so the required number of contracts is approximately 99,005/69.1377 = 1,432. The identity of the CTD security matters a great deal: had the CTD instead been the 10-year T-note, with a BPV of 81.6607 and a conversion factor of 0.8516, the futures BPV would be 81.6607/0.8516 = 95.8909 and only 99,005/95.8909 = 1,032 contracts would be required. A difference of 400 futures contracts is significant, so the asset manager must identify the CTD T-note before sizing a derivatives overlay.
rationales.C: This divides the BPV gap by the cheapest-to-deliver security's own BPV without adjusting for the conversion factor: (117,824 − 18,819)/56.8727 = 1,741. The hedging instrument is the futures contract, not the CTD note itself, and the futures BPV is the CTD BPV divided by the conversion factor: 56.8727/0.8226 = 69.1377. Using that figure gives 99,005/69.1377 = 1,432 contracts.

questions.stem: The conversion factors for Treasury note futures contracts are most likely based on:

options.A: an arbitrary yield to maturity of 8.00%.
options.B: each qualifying note's current market yield to maturity.
options.C: an arbitrary yield to maturity of 6.00%.

rationales.A: The standardized conversion-factor assumption is a yield to maturity of 6.00%, not 8.00%. The level of the assumption is not cosmetic: because the factors are computed off a fixed 6.00% yield, an eligible T-note with a coupon rate below 6.00% has a conversion factor less than 1.0000 and one with a coupon above 6.00% has a factor more than 1.0000. The same assumption also drives which security is cheapest to deliver when market yields sit well away from 6.00%.
rationales.B: Conversion factors rest on a fixed, arbitrary 6.00% yield to maturity rather than on each note's prevailing market yield. That is precisely what makes them standing, published numbers that render the qualifying T-notes roughly equivalent for delivery by the contract seller, the short position. Factors recomputed from each note's current market yield would move continuously and would remove the delivery option's economic content, since the short position's choice of which note to deliver arises from the mismatch between the fixed 6.00% assumption and actual market yields.
rationales.C: Conversion factors, which are used to make the qualifying T-notes roughly equivalent for delivery by the contract seller, or short position, are based on an arbitrary yield to maturity of 6.00%. If the eligible T-note has a coupon rate below (above) 6.00%, the conversion factor is less (more) than 1.0000. The invoice price paid by the buyer of the contract, the long position, at the expiration of the contract is the futures price multiplied by the conversion factor, plus accrued interest. Because the factors assume 6.00%, when market yields are below 6.00% the cheapest-to-deliver security is typically the qualifying T-note with the lowest duration; the 10-year T-note futures contract has therefore effectively been acting as a 6.5-year contract, which is what motivated the introduction of the Ultra 10-year contract as a hedging instrument more closely tied to the 10-year T-note traded in the cash market.

questions.stem: Contingent immunization is most likely:

options.A: a purely passive strategy at any funding level.
options.B: a hybrid passive-active strategy.
options.C: a passive strategy that turns active once the surplus is exhausted.

rationales.A: Contingent immunization is a hybrid rather than a purely passive strategy, and the funding level is exactly what determines how much discretion the manager has. While the surplus is above a designated threshold, the manager may pursue active strategies as if operating under a total return mandate. Only if the actively managed assets perform poorly and the surplus evaporates does the mandate revert to the purely passive strategy of building a duration-matching portfolio and managing it to remain on duration target.
rationales.B: The presence of a significant surplus allows the asset manager to consider a hybrid passive-active strategy known as contingent immunization. The manager can pursue active investment strategies, as if operating under a total return mandate, as long as the surplus is above a designated threshold. If the actively managed assets perform poorly and the surplus evaporates, the mandate reverts to the purely passive strategy of building a duration-matching portfolio and then managing it to remain on duration target. While the surplus is above a sufficient threshold, the manager may in principle increase portfolio risk in any asset category, including equity, fixed income, and alternative investments, and could also buy out-of-the-money commodity options contracts or credit default swaps. The objective is to attain portfolio gains that reduce the cost of retiring the debt obligations without falling below the minimum funding threshold. Liquidity is an important criterion in selecting those investments, because the positions will need to be unwound if losses cause the surplus to approach the threshold.
rationales.C: This reverses the trigger. Active management is permitted while the surplus sits above the designated threshold, and the strategy reverts to a passive duration-matching portfolio if losses erode the surplus toward the minimum funding level. Taking active risk after the surplus has been exhausted would be the opposite of the strategy's logic, since there would no longer be any cushion to absorb a loss on the active positions.

questions.stem: A corporation plans to retire its outstanding debt liabilities and is weighing a bond tender offer, cash flow matching with government bonds, and duration matching with high-quality corporate bonds plus an interest rate derivatives overlay. Regarding these three alternatives, it is most likely that:

options.A: accounting defeasement would be granted for duration matching but not for cash flow matching.
options.B: the tender offer would be made at a premium above the market price.
options.C: the tender offer would be made at a discount below the market price.

rationales.A: The defeasement outcomes are reversed. Accounting defeasement is highly likely to be allowed for the cash flow matching alternative, because the purchased securities are government bonds that match the coupon interest and principal redemptions on the debt liabilities closely enough for the auditors to permit removing both the defeasing asset portfolio and the liabilities from the balance sheet. It is very unlikely to be allowed for duration matching, where the assets are high-quality corporate bonds whose duration is kept on target with interest rate derivatives contracts as time passes and yields change — a position that must be actively maintained and does not replicate the liability cash flows.
rationales.B: A bond tender offer buys back the debt liabilities on the open market at a premium above the market price. The premium would have to be at a price commensurate with a triple-A rating to entice the bondholders to sell, since holders have no obligation to tender and will only do so if compensated above what the market will pay them. The two alternatives differ in balance sheet treatment: cash flow matching with government bonds is highly likely to qualify for accounting defeasement, allowing both the asset portfolio and the liabilities to be removed from the balance sheet, whereas duration matching with corporate bonds and a derivatives overlay is very unlikely to qualify.
rationales.C: A tender offer below the market price would attract no bonds. Holders of a high-quality credit can simply sell in the open market at the prevailing price instead, so the offer must be at a premium above the market price — at a level commensurate with a triple-A rating — to induce them to tender.

questions.stem: When the market values of the assets and the liabilities differ, the asset portfolio chosen for duration matching is most likely the one with:

options.A: money duration matched to the liabilities and the highest convexity available.
options.B: money duration closest to the liabilities and convexity below theirs.
options.C: money duration matched to the liabilities and the lowest convexity above theirs.

rationales.A: Asset convexity must exceed that of the liabilities, but maximizing it is the wrong objective. Among the portfolios that satisfy the condition, the one with the lowest convexity still above the liabilities' should be chosen, because higher convexity comes with greater dispersion of cash flows and therefore greater structural risk — exposure to shifts and twists in the yield curve that a parallel-shift money duration match does not neutralize. The benchmark is the zero-coupon bond that would provide perfect immunization: the chosen portfolio should sit as close to it as the condition permits, not as far from it as possible.
rationales.B: This is the exact error to avoid. When market values differ, duration matching entails matching money durations, in particular basis point values, and two candidate portfolios can both have BPVs close to the liabilities'. It is incorrect to choose one simply because its BPV is numerically closer. The decisive difference lies in the convexities: to immunize multiple liabilities, the convexity and the dispersion of cash flows of the assets must be greater than those of the liabilities, so a portfolio whose convexity falls below the liabilities' fails the immunization conditions no matter how close its BPV happens to be.
rationales.C: Duration matching when the market values of the assets and the liabilities differ entails matching the money durations, in particular the basis point values. Among portfolios with BPVs close to the liabilities', the important difference lies in the convexities. To immunize multiple liabilities, the convexity and the dispersion of cash flows of the assets need to be greater than those of the liabilities, but the portfolio chosen should have the lowest convexity available that still meets that condition, in order to minimize the structural risk to the strategy. The correct immunizing portfolio is therefore the lower-convexity one whose convexity nonetheless exceeds that of the liabilities, while remaining above the convexity of the zero-coupon bond that would provide perfect immunization.

questions.stem: A synthetic barbell strategy for immunizing a long-dated liability most likely consists of:

options.A: cash and derivatives positions concentrated at the horizon-matching point.
options.B: positions in the short-term and longer-term segments of the curve.
options.C: cash bond positions at both ends of the curve, with no derivatives.

rationales.A: That describes a bullet structure rather than a barbell. In the synthetic barbell the underlying cash portfolio sits in the short-term market while the derivatives exposure sits at a longer segment of the curve, so the two legs are deliberately split rather than concentrated at the horizon-matching point. Spreading the futures across additional segments, such as the actively traded two-year and five-year Treasury contracts, moves the structure further away from a single-point concentration and reduces structural risk arising from non-parallel shifts and twists.
rationales.B: A synthetic barbell has positions in both the short-term and the longer-term segments of the yield curve, and the term synthetic means created with derivatives. The underlying asset portfolio is concentrated in the short-term market, while the derivatives portfolio is either at the 6.5-year or the 10-year segment of the yield curve. Because actively traded two-year and five-year Treasury futures contracts also exist, the asset manager could choose to spread the futures contracts across other segments of the yield curve. That diversification reduces the structural risk to the immunization strategy arising from non-parallel shifts and twists to the curve.
rationales.C: The strategy is called synthetic precisely because the longer-term exposure is created with derivatives rather than with cash bonds. The underlying cash portfolio is concentrated in the short-term market, and the long leg comes from futures positions at the 6.5-year or 10-year segment, so a derivatives-free holding of cash bonds at both ends of the curve is not the structure being described.

questions.stem: Type I cash flows are most likely those for which:

options.A: both the scheduled amounts and the payment dates are known.
options.B: neither the scheduled amounts nor the payment dates are known.
options.C: the scheduled amounts are known but the payment dates are uncertain.

rationales.A: Type I cash flows are those for which the scheduled amounts and the payment dates are both known to the asset manager. That is the assumption carried through the single-liability and multiple-liability immunization contexts. Even so, measurement error for asset BPV can arise in the classic immunization strategy for Type I cash flows, which have set amounts and dates. Higher liability types relax the assumption: more, and harder-to-make, assumptions are needed to deal with Type IV liabilities, and they lead to greater uncertainty regarding the models' outputs.
rationales.B: Amounts and dates that are both unknown describe Type IV liabilities, the opposite of the fully known Type I case, and it is precisely those added assumptions that create greater uncertainty in the models' outputs.
rationales.C: Known amounts paired with uncertain payment timing describe a higher liability type. Type I cash flows require both the scheduled amounts and the payment dates to be known to the asset manager.

questions.stem: A pension plan holds $2.700 billion of assets allocated 50% to equity, 40% to fixed income with a modified duration of 5.5, and 10% to alternatives. The asset basis point value (BPV) is closest to:

rationales.A: $742,500 applies the 5.5 modified duration to the 40% fixed-income allocation plus the 10% alternatives allocation, a combined weight of 0.50: $2.700 billion x (0.50 x 5.5) x 0.0001 = $742,500. Alternatives, like equity, are assumed to have zero effective duration, so the 10% sleeve contributes nothing to the duration-weighted calculation.
rationales.B: Asset BPV = $2.700 billion x [(0.50 x 0) + (0.40 x 5.5) + (0.10 x 0)] x 0.0001 = $594,000. The term in brackets is the estimated effective duration for the asset portfolio, calculated using the shares of market value as the weights. Equity duration and alternatives duration are assumed to be zero because, to be conservative, no stable and predictable relationship is assumed between valuations on those asset classes and market interest rates; assuming zero duration does not imply that equity and alternatives have no interest rate risk. The plan is therefore running a significant duration gap, because the asset BPV of $594,000 is much lower than the liability BPV of $2,257,080 under the projected benefit obligation measure.
rationales.C: $1,485,000 applies the 5.5 fixed-income duration to the entire portfolio: $2.700 billion x 5.5 x 0.0001 = $1,485,000. That ignores the assignment of zero effective duration to equity and to alternatives, so it treats all of market value as duration-bearing when only the 40% fixed-income allocation is.

questions.stem: A pension plan with liability BPV of $2,257,080 and asset BPV of $594,000 buys 17,343 Ultra 10-year T-note futures contracts (futures BPV $95.8909) to close its duration gap. If 10-year Treasury yields rise by 5 bps, the realized daily mark-to-market loss on the futures position is closest to:

options.A: $1.663 million.
options.B: $8.315 million.
options.C: $16.630 million.

rationales.A: $1.663 million is the mark-to-market loss for a 1 bp move: $95.8909 x 1 x 17,343 = $1.663 million. The yield change given is 5 bps, so the realized loss that day is five times this figure.
rationales.B: The contracts needed to fully hedge the interest rate risk created by the duration gap are N_f = (2,257,080 - 594,000)/95.8909 = 17,343. Given a futures BPV of $95.8909 per contract, a 5 bp rise in 10-year Treasury yields produces a realized loss that day of $95.8909 x 5 x 17,343 = $8,315,179, or more than $8.315 million. One concern with hedging with futures is the need for daily oversight of the positions, which arises because futures contracts are marked to market and settled at the end of each trading day into the margin account. The realized cash loss is offset by an unrealized reduction in the present value of the liabilities, but a futures position this large leads to significant daily cash flows.
rationales.C: $16.630 million corresponds to a 10 bp move, double the 5 bps given: $95.8909 x 10 x 17,343 = $16.630 million.

questions.stem: A pension plan whose asset BPV is below its liability BPV closes the duration gap with a receive-fixed interest rate swap. In the duration-gap relationship, the swap's hedging basis point value is most likely:

options.A: subtracted from asset BPV, scaled per 100 of notional principal.
options.B: added to asset BPV, scaled per 100 of notional principal.
options.C: added to asset BPV, scaled by 100 times the notional principal.

rationales.A: A receive-fixed swap carries positive duration, so its hedging BPV is added to the asset BPV rather than subtracted from it. The risk statistics for an interest rate swap can be obtained by interpreting the contract as a combination of bonds: from the pension fund's perspective, the swap is viewed as buying a 30-year, 4.16% fixed-rate bond from the swap dealer and financing that purchase by issuing a 30-year floating-rate note (FRN) that pays the three-month MRR. The swap's money duration is taken to be the (high) duration of the fixed-rate bond minus the (low) duration of the FRN, which is why a receive-fixed swap has positive duration. Subtracting the swap term would widen the plan's negative duration gap instead of closing it.
rationales.B: The relationship is Asset BPV + [NP x Swap BPV/100] = Liability BPV. The swap term is added because a receive-fixed swap has positive duration, and it is divided by 100 because swap BPV is quoted per 100 of notional principal. The risk statistics for an interest rate swap can be obtained by interpreting the contract as a combination of bonds: from the pension fund's perspective, the swap is viewed as buying a 30-year, 4.16% fixed-rate bond from the swap dealer and financing that purchase by issuing a 30-year floating-rate note (FRN) that pays the three-month MRR. The swap's money duration is taken to be the (high) duration of the fixed-rate bond minus the (low) duration of the FRN, which explains the positive duration of a receive-fixed swap. From the swap dealer's perspective, the contract is viewed as purchasing a (low duration) FRN financed by issuing a (high duration) fixed-rate bond, so the swap has negative duration to the dealer.
rationales.C: Swap BPV is quoted per 100 of notional principal, so the notional is divided by 100, not multiplied by it. Scaling by 100 times the notional overstates the swap's hedging BPV by a factor of 10,000 and would call for a notional far smaller than the one needed to close the gap.

questions.stem: A pension fund has asset BPV of $594,000 and liability BPV of $2,257,080 (PBO measure). To close the duration gap to zero, it enters a 30-year receive-fixed interest rate swap (fixed rate 4.16%) with a BPV of 0.1673 per 100 of notional. The required notional principal is closest to:

options.A: $994 million.
options.B: $166 million.
options.C: $9.94 million.

rationales.A: The notional principal (NP) needed to close the duration gap to zero satisfies Asset BPV + [NP x Swap BPV/100] = Liability BPV, an expression similar to the one used for futures contracts. With an asset BPV of $594,000 and a liability BPV of $2,257,080 under the projected benefit obligation measure, and a swap BPV of 0.1673 per 100 of notional: 594,000 + [NP x 0.1673/100] = 2,257,080, so NP = 994,070,532, or about $994 million. A receive-fixed swap has positive duration, so when swap rates fall the receive-fixed position gains value, and the hedging fund uses that gain to offset the balance sheet losses that falling rates produce.
rationales.B: $166 million comes from multiplying the BPV gap by 100 without dividing by the swap BPV: 1,663,080 x 100 = 166,308,000. The required notional is NP = (2,257,080 - 594,000)/(0.1673/100) = 994,070,532.
rationales.C: $9.94 million results from dividing the BPV gap by 0.1673 without recognizing that the swap BPV is quoted per 100 of notional: 1,663,080/0.1673 = 9,941,303, a factor of 100 too small.

questions.stem: The interest rate hedging ratio is most likely a measure of:

options.A: the share of plan assets held in cash to meet liquidity needs.
options.B: the ratio of asset portfolio convexity to liability portfolio convexity.
options.C: the extent of interest rate risk management.

rationales.A: This confuses the hedging ratio with a liquidity reserve. The hedging ratio indicates the extent of interest rate risk management, not the portion of plan assets set aside in cash for near-term benefit payments.
rationales.B: The hedging ratio runs from 0% to 100% and concerns the degree to which duration, measured by BPV, is hedged. It is not a comparison of asset convexity with liability convexity.
rationales.C: The term hedging ratio, or interest rate hedging ratio since the focus is on reducing interest rate risk, indicates the extent of interest rate risk management. A hedging ratio of 0% indicates no hedging at all, so the pension plan retains its significant negative duration gap and the risk of lower corporate bond yields. A hedging ratio of 100% indicates an attempt to fully balance, or to immunize, the assets and liabilities; for the plan in question that means entering the receive-fixed swap for a notional principal of $994 million. In practice, partial hedges are common, and the manager's task is to select the hedging ratio between 0% and 100%. Interest rate swaps typically have a value of zero at initiation, which is part of why they are convenient instruments for setting that ratio.

questions.stem: Strategic hedging in a liability-driven mandate is most likely:

options.A: maintaining a hedging ratio of 100% regardless of the rate outlook.
options.B: actively managing the hedging ratio.
options.C: hedging the strategic asset allocation but not tactical positions.

rationales.A: A static full hedge is the opposite of strategic hedging. Under strategic hedging the sponsor grants a range, so the ratio is varied with the manager's rate view rather than pinned at full immunization; a fixed 100% ratio is simply the preset-hedging-ratio strategy against which strategic hedging decisions are measured.
rationales.B: Strategic hedging is active management of the hedging ratio: the plan sponsor allows the manager some flexibility in selecting it, for example a mandate to stay within a range of 25% to 75%. When the manager anticipates lower market rates, and therefore gains on receive-fixed interest rate swaps, the manager prefers to be at the top of the allowable range. If market swap rates are expected to go up, the manager could reduce the hedging ratio to the lower end of the range. The performance of the strategic hedging decisions can be measured against a strategy of maintaining a preset hedging ratio, for instance 50%.
rationales.C: This conflates strategic hedging with strategic asset allocation. Strategic hedging refers to flexibility in the hedging ratio itself, within a range set by the sponsor, not to hedging one slice of the asset allocation while leaving another slice unhedged.

questions.stem: For a pension plan closing a negative duration gap, the alternatives to a receive-fixed interest rate swap most likely consist of:

options.A: no alternative instrument.
options.B: the sale of equities to buy long-dated bonds only.
options.C: a purchased receiver swaption or a swaption collar.

rationales.A: Alternatives do exist: a purchased receiver swaption and a swaption collar are both developed as alternatives to the receive-fixed swap, so saying there is none is incorrect.
rationales.B: The derivative alternatives, the purchased receiver swaption and the swaption collar, add hedging BPV without reallocating the asset portfolio, so selling equities to buy long-dated bonds is not the only route to closing the gap.
rationales.C: An alternative to the receive-fixed interest rate swap is a purchased receiver swaption, which confers to the buyer the right to enter the swap as the fixed-rate receiver. Because of its negative duration gap, with asset BPV less than liability BPV, the typical pension plan suffers when interest rates fall and could become underfunded; the gain on the receiver swaption as rates decline offsets the losses on the balance sheet, although the option premium has to be paid up front. Another alternative is a swaption collar, the combination of buying the receiver swaption and writing a payer swaption, where the premium received on the payer swaption that is written offsets the premium needed to buy the receiver swaption.

questions.stem: The choice among a receive-fixed swap, a purchased receiver swaption, and a swaption collar most likely depends on:

options.A: the manager's view on future interest rates.
options.B: the relative transaction costs of the instruments alone.
options.C: the size of the plan's funding surplus alone.

rationales.A: The choice among hedging with the receive-fixed swap, the purchased receiver swaption, and the swaption collar depends in part on the pension fund manager's view on future interest rates. If rates are expected to be low, the receive-fixed swap typically is the preferred derivative. If rates are expected to go up, the receiver swaption can become attractive. And if rates are projected to reach a certain threshold that depends on the option costs and the strike rates, the swaption collar can become the favored choice.
rationales.B: Transaction costs and premiums matter, but they are not the whole story: the choice hinges primarily on the manager's view of future rates, which is what determines whether the swap, the swaption, or the collar performs best. Option costs and strike rates enter only as the threshold at which the collar becomes favored.
rationales.C: The size of the funding surplus governs contingent immunization capacity, whereas the choice of instrument turns on the interest rate outlook, with option costs and strike rates setting the point at which the collar is preferred.

questions.stem: With respect to a steepening twist in the high-quality bond yield curve, it is most likely that:

options.A: the scenario is not specified at individual maturities.
options.B: short-term yields fall while long-term yields rise.
options.C: outcomes are identical across the curve.

rationales.A: The steepening twist is fully specified point by point along the curve: the 1.5-year yield is assumed to drop by 25 bps, the 6-year yield remains the same, and the 11.5-year yield goes up by 25 bps. Because those assumed changes differ by maturity, the scenario has definite and distinct effects on each side of the balance sheet, which is what makes it possible to value the twist at all.
rationales.B: In a steepening twist, short-term yields on high-quality bonds go down while long-term yields go up. The 1.5-year yield is assumed to drop by 25 bps, the 6-year yield remains the same, and the 11.5-year yield goes up by 25 bps. These changes lead to a loss of EUR1,178,071 in the asset portfolio as its cash flow yield increases by 10.04 bps. The market value of the liabilities drops by only EUR835,156, because the liability cash flow yield increases by only 7.11 bps. The value of the assets therefore goes down by more than the value of the liabilities, and the difference, EUR342,915, is the loss. The twist to the shape of the yield curve, rather than a parallel shift, is the source of that loss.
rationales.C: Yield changes vary by maturity in a twist, so positions at different points on the curve do not fare alike. The asset portfolio's cash flow yield rises 10.04 bps and the portfolio loses EUR1,178,071, while the liability cash flow yield rises only 7.11 bps and liability value falls EUR835,156, leaving a net loss of EUR342,915. Identical outcomes would require the yield changes themselves to be identical, which is exactly what a twist rules out.

questions.stem: A pension plan reports an ABO of $1.730 billion with effective duration 17.1 and a PBO of $2.687 billion with effective duration 8.4. For a corporate sponsor that sees itself as an ongoing independent institution preserving the plan's current design, the appropriate liability BPV is closest to:

rationales.A: $4,594,770 pairs the PBO market value with the ABO's effective duration: $2.687 billion × 17.1 × 0.0001. Each liability measure carries its own market value and its own effective duration, so the inputs cannot be mixed. Computed consistently, ABO BPV = $1.730 billion × 17.1 × 0.0001 = $2,958,300 and PBO BPV = $2.687 billion × 8.4 × 0.0001 = $2,257,080.
rationales.B: $2,958,300 is the ABO BPV: $1.730 billion × 17.1 × 0.0001. The accumulated benefit obligation is based on current wages, and it is the measure that matters more when, for example, the corporation anticipates that it might be an acquisition target and that the acquirer would likely want to convert the retirement plan from defined benefit to defined contribution. A sponsor that sees itself as an ongoing independent institution preserving the plan's current design should instead use the projected benefit obligation, whose BPV is $2.687 billion × 8.4 × 0.0001 = $2,257,080.
rationales.C: The projected benefit obligation is based on expected future wage levels, and it is the appropriate liability measure for a corporate sponsor that sees itself as an ongoing independent institution preserving the pension plan's current design. PBO BPV = $2.687 billion × 8.4 × 0.0001 = $2,257,080. The alternative measure, the accumulated benefit obligation, is based on current wages and gives ABO BPV = $1.730 billion × 17.1 × 0.0001 = $2,958,300; it would matter more if the sponsor expected to be acquired and the plan converted from defined benefit to defined contribution. There is a significant difference between liabilities of $1.730 billion with an effective duration of 17.1 and liabilities of $2.687 billion with an effective duration of 8.4, and the plan sponsor must decide which measure to use for risk management and asset allocation.

questions.stem: When interest rate risk is fully hedged, the change in the market value of the liabilities is most likely matched by the change in the value of:

options.A: neither the assets nor the hedge.
options.B: the assets alone.
options.C: the assets and the hedge.

rationales.A: The relationship is stated explicitly across all three components: Asset BPV × ΔAsset yields + Hedge BPV × ΔHedge yields ≈ Liability BPV × ΔLiability yields, where the yield changes are measured in basis points. Far from there being no such relationship, it is precisely this expression that identifies the sources of risk to a liability-driven investing strategy.
rationales.B: Matching asset BPV to liability BPV alone is the special case in which there is no derivatives overlay. The hedge term is integral to the general relationship: Asset BPV × ΔAsset yields + Hedge BPV × ΔHedge yields ≈ Liability BPV × ΔLiability yields. When futures or swaps are used, it is the combined money duration of the asset portfolio and the hedge that must match the money duration of the liabilities.
rationales.C: Full hedging is described by Asset BPV × ΔAsset yields + Hedge BPV × ΔHedge yields ≈ Liability BPV × ΔLiability yields, with ΔAsset yields, ΔHedge yields and ΔLiability yields measured in basis points. This equation describes an immunization strategy, a hedging ratio of 100%, whereby the intent is to match the changes in market value on each side of the balance sheet when yields change; doing so entails matching the money duration of assets and liabilities. Entities also choose to partially hedge interest rate risk by selecting a hedging ratio of less than 100%, but in any case the relationship indicates the source of the risks to liability-driven investing. The "approximately equals" sign results from ignoring higher-order terms, such as convexity.

questions.stem: Model risk in a liability-driven investing framework most likely arises from:

options.A: a counterparty's failure to perform on a hedging derivative.
options.B: assumptions about the future and approximated parameters.
options.C: transaction costs eroding the tracking of liabilities.

rationales.A: A counterparty failing to perform on a derivative is counterparty, or credit, risk. Model risk is something else: it is encountered whenever assumptions are made about future events and approximations are used to measure key parameters, and the risk is that those assumptions turn out to be wrong and the approximations are inaccurate.
rationales.B: Model risk is encountered in financial modeling whenever assumptions are made about future events and approximations are used to measure key parameters. The risk is that those assumptions turn out to be wrong and the approximations are inaccurate. In a defined benefit pension plan setting, for instance, the effective durations for investments in equity and alternative assets are assumed to be zero. That assumption introduces the risk that asset BPV is mis-measured if, in fact, those market values do change as the yield curve shifts. The modeling problem is that the effect on those asset classes is not predictable or stable, because it depends on the reason for the change in nominal interest rates: unlike fixed-income bonds, an increase in expected inflation can have a very different effect on equity and alternative asset valuations than an increase in the real rate.
rationales.C: Transaction-cost drag is a distinct source of underperformance against a liability benchmark. Model risk concerns the validity of the modeling assumptions and the accuracy of the parameter estimates, such as assuming zero effective duration for equity and alternative assets, not the frictions incurred in trading the portfolio.

questions.stem: In the classic immunization strategy for Type I cash flows, asset BPV is most likely:

options.A: free of measurement error.
options.B: approximated by a weighted average of component durations.
options.C: insensitive to the duration measure chosen.

rationales.A: Measurement error for asset BPV can arise even in the classic immunization strategy for Type I cash flows, which have set amounts and dates. Certainty about the amounts and the dates of the liability cash flows does not remove the error introduced by the way the asset portfolio's duration is measured.
rationales.B: In practice, it is common to approximate the asset portfolio duration using the weighted average of the individual durations for the component bonds, and that approximation is a source of measurement error even for Type I cash flows, which have set amounts and dates. A better approach to achieve immunization uses the cash flow yield to discount the future coupon and principal payments. The error from the weighted-average shortcut is minimized when the underlying yield curve is flat or when future cash flows are concentrated in the flattest segment of the curve.
rationales.C: The duration measure chosen does matter. The weighted average of the component bonds' durations is only an approximation of the portfolio's sensitivity and differs from the cash flow yield approach, which discounts the future coupon and principal payments. The resulting error is minimized when the underlying yield curve is flat or when future cash flows are concentrated in the flattest segment of the curve, which is to say it is not zero in general.

questions.stem: When derivatives overlays are used to immunize, the futures BPV applied in the hedge is most likely:

options.A: known exactly from the contract's fixed sensitivities.
options.B: free of measurement risk.
options.C: estimated from the cheapest-to-deliver bond and its conversion factor.

rationales.A: The futures BPV is estimated rather than read off the contract. The common approximation takes it to be the BPV for the qualifying cheapest-to-deliver security divided by its conversion factor. A more developed calculation involving short-term rates and accrued interest could change the number of contracts needed to hedge the interest rate risk, and the cheapest-to-deliver security itself can change over the life of the hedge.
rationales.B: A measurement problem arises in hedge BPV just as it does in asset BPV. The futures BPV is an estimate, obtained as the BPV for the qualifying cheapest-to-deliver security divided by its conversion factor. Although the error introduced by using that approximation might not be large, it still can be a source of underperformance in the hedging strategy, so the overlay is not free of measurement risk.
rationales.C: When derivatives overlays are used to immunize, a common approximation estimates the futures BPV to be the BPV for the qualifying cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) security divided by its conversion factor. A more developed calculation involving short-term rates and accrued interest, however, could change the number of contracts needed to hedge the interest rate risk. Although the error introduced by using the approximation might not be large, it still can be a source of underperformance in the hedging strategy.

questions.stem: With respect to measuring the liability BPV of a defined benefit pension plan, it is most likely that:

options.A: longevity risk is eliminated by using the ABO.
options.B: the exercise is a difficult modeling problem.
options.C: the ABO requires more assumptions than the PBO.

rationales.A: Longevity risk stems from the difficulty in projecting the life spans of the retirees covered by the plan: the risk is that the sponsor has not provided sufficient assets to make a longer-than-expected payout stream. That difficulty affects both liability measures. Choosing the accumulated benefit obligation over the projected benefit obligation changes the wage assumption, not the uncertainty surrounding the length of the payout horizon.
rationales.B: Measuring a defined benefit pension plan's liability is clearly a difficult financial modeling problem, and model risk in obtaining liability BPV follows from it. Even the simple models for the two liability measures, the ABO and the PBO, necessarily require many assumptions about the future, including the dates when employees retire and their wage levels at those times. The difficulty in projecting the life spans of retirees covered by the plan leads to longevity risk, the risk that the sponsor has not provided sufficient assets to make the longer-than-expected payout stream. More, and harder-to-make, assumptions are needed to deal with Type IV liabilities, and they lead to greater uncertainty regarding the models' outputs.
rationales.C: This reverses the two definitions: the projected benefit obligation incorporates expected future wage levels, while the accumulated benefit obligation is based on current wages. Both measures still require many assumptions about the future, including the dates when employees retire and the life spans of the retirees covered by the plan, so neither escapes the modeling problem.

questions.stem: In hedging a portfolio's interest rate risk against its liabilities, matching asset, hedge and liability BPVs most likely assumes that:

options.A: all yields change by the same percentage amount.
options.B: assets and liabilities have identical cash flow dispersion.
options.C: all yields change by the same number of basis points.

rationales.A: The implicit assumption is that all yields change by the same number of basis points, not by the same percentage amount: ΔAsset yields, ΔHedge yields and ΔLiability yields are taken to be equal in basis points. Equal percentage changes would imply larger absolute moves at higher yield levels, which is not the assumption embedded in matching money duration.
rationales.B: Minimizing the dispersion of cash flows in the asset portfolio mitigates the risk of non-parallel shifts, and immunization calls for asset cash flow dispersion to exceed that of the liabilities rather than match it. The assumption implicit in matching the BPVs is a different one: that all yields change by the same number of basis points.
rationales.C: Implicit in matching Asset BPV, Hedge BPV and Liability BPV is the assumption that all yields change by the same number of basis points, that is, that ΔAsset yields, ΔHedge yields and ΔLiability yields are equal. That is a strong assumption, and a source of risk, if the fixed-income assets, the derivatives and the liabilities are positioned at varying points along the benchmark bond yield curve and at varying spreads to that curve. In immunizing the interest rate risk on a single liability with a portfolio of fixed-income bonds, a parallel yield curve shift is a sufficient but not a necessary condition to achieve the desired outcome. Non-parallel shifts and twists to the yield curve can result in changes to the cash flow yield on the immunizing portfolio that do not match the change in the yield on the zero-coupon bond that would provide perfect immunization. Minimizing dispersion of the cash flows in the asset portfolio mitigates this risk.

questions.stem: With respect to spread risk in a liability-driven investing framework, it is most likely that:

options.A: asset and liability discount rates cannot diverge.
options.B: assets and liabilities track the same yield curve.
options.C: the relevant yields are corporate rather than government.

rationales.A: The framework for thinking about interest rate risk rests on changes in the benchmark bond yield curve, usually the government bond curve, but the rates that actually matter can and do diverge from it. A pension fund may hold a portfolio tracking a well-diversified corporate bond index that includes non-investment-grade securities, while the present value of retirement benefits depends on yields on high-quality corporate bonds. The two sets of spreads need not move in unison.
rationales.B: Asset yields and liability discount rates often move by different amounts than benchmark government yields, and by different amounts from each other. The risk is that the respective spreads on the broad index held in the portfolio and on the high-quality sector used to discount the liabilities do not move in unison with a shift in the government bond yield curve. That divergence is spread risk, and it is also present when immunizing multiple Type I liabilities.
rationales.C: Generally, the framework for thinking about interest rate risk rests on changes in the benchmark bond yield curve, which usually is the yield curve for government bonds. In practice, however, ΔAsset yield and ΔLiability yield often refer to various classes of corporate bonds. In a pension fund example, the fund holds a portfolio of fixed-income bonds that tracks a well-diversified index of corporate bonds that may include non-investment-grade securities, while the present value of retirement benefits depends on yields on high-quality corporate bonds. A risk is therefore that the respective spreads on the broad index and the high-quality sector do not move in unison with a shift in the government bond yield curve. A similar spread risk is present when immunizing multiple Type I liabilities.

questions.stem: Compared with yields on more-liquid Treasuries, yields on high-quality corporate bonds are most likely:

options.A: equally volatile.
options.B: less volatile.
options.C: more volatile.

rationales.A: Equal volatility would leave no basis risk from the corporate/Treasury spread, but the volatilities are not equal. Government bonds are used in a wide variety of hedging as well as speculative trading strategies by institutional investors, and inflows of international funds typically are placed in government bonds, at least until they are allocated to other asset classes. Those factors lead to greater volatility in Treasury yields than in comparable-maturity corporate bonds, which is a source of risk when Treasury futures hedge corporate obligations.
rationales.B: Usually, yields on high-quality corporate bonds are less volatile than on more-liquid Treasuries. Government bonds are used in a wide variety of hedging as well as speculative trading strategies by institutional investors. Also, inflows of international funds typically are placed in government bonds, at least until they are allocated to other asset classes. Those factors lead to greater volatility in Treasury yields than comparable-maturity corporate bonds. The gap matters for derivatives overlay strategies: when futures contracts on 10-year US Treasury notes are used to hedge liabilities that are corporate obligations, whether passively or contingently, movements in the corporate/Treasury yield spread introduce risk to the hedging strategy.
rationales.C: This reverses the relationship. High-quality corporate yields are usually less volatile than those on the more heavily traded Treasuries, which are used in a wide variety of hedging and speculative trading strategies and which absorb inflows of international funds until those funds are allocated elsewhere. Those factors lead to greater volatility in Treasury yields than comparable-maturity corporate bonds.
