questions.stem: Under contingent immunization, if losses reduce the surplus to its minimum amount, the manager is most likely to:

options.A: revert to a passive duration-matching portfolio of high-quality bonds.
options.B: wait until the liability due date to unwind the active positions.
options.C: retain distressed holdings as long as portfolio BPV stays matched.

rationales.A: Contingent immunization lets the manager increase portfolio risk through active management while the surplus sits above the stated threshold. If losses reduce that surplus to some minimum amount, the positions need to be adjusted to revert to a passive duration-matching fixed-income portfolio of high-quality bonds. Because the trigger can be reached at any time, the actively managed positions may have to be unwound quickly, which makes liquidity an important criterion in selecting them in the first place. Distressed assets that become hard to value, such as tranches of subprime mortgage-backed securities, also become illiquid during financial crises, so they are hardest to sell at a fair price at exactly the moment the reversion is required.
rationales.B: Reversion is triggered whenever losses reduce the surplus to the minimum threshold, which can happen at any time rather than only at the liability due date. Positions may therefore need to be unwound quickly and at short notice, so the liquidity of the actively managed holdings is an important criterion in selecting the investments, not an irrelevance.
rationales.C: The portfolio reverted to is a passive duration-matching portfolio of high-quality bonds. Distressed, hard-to-value assets such as subprime MBS tranches become illiquid during financial crises and would have to be liquidated, potentially at unfavorable prices; a matched portfolio BPV does not cure the credit quality and liquidity problem that makes them unsuitable for the immunizing portfolio.

questions.stem: In managing interest rate risk relative to liabilities, an LDI manager is most likely to:

options.A: choose between asset allocation and a derivatives overlay.
options.B: prefer a derivatives overlay in all circumstances.
options.C: avoid Treasury STRIPS when closing a duration gap.

rationales.A: An LDI manager has a fundamental choice between managing interest rate risk with asset allocation and with derivatives overlays. As with all financial management decisions, the choice depends on a thorough evaluation of risk and return trade-offs. In some circumstances, derivatives might be deemed too expensive or risky, particularly regarding available collateral and cash holdings. The manager might then choose instead to increase holdings of long-term, high-quality bonds that have high duration statistics. The growth of government zero-coupon bonds, such as US Treasury STRIPS (Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities), facilitates that asset reallocation process.
rationales.B: This reverses the caveat attached to derivatives: an overlay might be deemed too expensive or too risky precisely because of the collateral and cash holdings it requires, and that is what can push the manager toward physical long-term, high-quality bonds with high duration statistics instead. Neither route dominates; the choice turns on a thorough evaluation of risk and return trade-offs.
rationales.C: STRIPS carry high duration statistics — a zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration equals its time to maturity, so a 30-year STRIP has a duration of about 30 — which is exactly why the growth of the STRIPS market facilitates closing a duration gap through asset reallocation rather than through a derivatives overlay.

questions.stem: A corporation seeking to monetize the call option embedded in its outstanding callable debt is most likely to:

options.A: write a receiver swaption.
options.B: take no action, as no swaption strategy applies.
options.C: repurchase the debt in the open market.

rationales.A: When the corporation issued the callable bond it effectively bought the call option, which gave it the flexibility to refinance at a lower cost of borrowed funds if benchmark rates and/or its own credit spread narrow. Writing a receiver swaption — an option giving the swaption buyer the right to enter into a swap to receive fixed and pay floating — sells that call option, and the corporation captures the value of the embedded call by means of the premium received. Suppose market rates in three years are higher than the strike rate on the swaption and the yield on the debt security: both options, the embedded call in the bond liability and the swaption, expire out of the money, and the asset and liability both have seven years until maturity and are non-callable. Suppose instead that market rates fall and bond prices go up: both options are now in the money, so the corporation sells the seven-year bonds held as assets and uses the proceeds to call the debt liabilities at par value, and the gain on that transaction offsets the loss on closing out the swaption with the counterparty.
rationales.B: A strategy does exist. Writing a receiver swaption monetizes the call option the issuer effectively bought when it issued callable debt: the premium is received today, and if rates fall, the gain from selling the bond assets and calling the liabilities at par offsets the loss on closing out the swaption.
rationales.C: An open-market repurchase is not the remedy at issue here. The embedded call the issuer already owns can be sold through a receiver swaption, with the premium received capturing its value, and if rates subsequently fall the call on the debt offsets the in-the-money swaption position.

drills.los_text: discuss bond indexes and the challenges of managing a fixed-income portfolio to mimic the characteristics of a bond index

questions.stem: Compared with global equity markets, global fixed-income markets are most likely:

options.A: similar in size, with comparable numbers of securities outstanding.
options.B: of indeterminate relative size.
options.C: much larger, with vastly more securities outstanding.

rationales.A: Fixed-income markets are much larger and broader, with vastly more securities outstanding. The MSCI World Index holds about 1,600 securities, against more than 16,000 in the Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate Index, so the security counts differ by roughly an order of magnitude rather than being comparable. Fixed-income issuers also represent a much wider range of borrowers than the relatively narrow universe of companies that issue equity.
rationales.B: The relative scale of the two markets is readily measured, and the comparison is explicit. Broad index constituent counts differ by roughly a factor of ten — about 1,600 securities in the MSCI World Index against more than 16,000 in the Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate — and a single issuer can have dozens of bonds outstanding against one class of common stock.
rationales.C: Fixed-income markets are much larger and broader than equity markets, and the number of fixed-income securities outstanding is vastly larger, as broad market indexes reflect. The MSCI World Index, which captures equities in 23 developed market countries and 85% of the available market capitalization in each market, consists of about 1,600 securities, whereas the Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate Index, covering global investment-grade debt from 24 local currency markets, consists of more than 16,000 securities. Those fixed-income issuers represent a much wider range of borrowers than the relatively narrow universe of companies issuing equity securities.

questions.stem: The Bloomberg Barclays US Aggregate Index is best described as:

options.A: a US Treasury-only index.
options.B: one of four regional aggregates within the Global Aggregate Index.
options.C: an index with no published constituent data.

rationales.A: The index spans several sectors, not Treasuries alone: US Treasuries, government agency securities, corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed securities, and commercial mortgage-backed securities. That breadth is what makes it one of the four regional aggregate benchmarks constituting the Global Aggregate.
rationales.B: The Bloomberg Barclays US Aggregate Index is the oldest and most widely recognized US bond market index, and it is one of four regional aggregate benchmarks that constitute the Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate Index. It includes US Treasuries, government agency securities, corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed securities, and commercial mortgage-backed securities. Although the large number of index constituents provides a means of risk diversification, in practice it is neither feasible nor cost-effective for investors to pursue a full replication approach with a broad fixed-income market index.
rationales.C: Constituent and sector composition is published and transparent, which is how investors know the index holds Treasuries, agencies, corporates, and the securitized sectors, and how they can judge that full replication of so broad a benchmark is neither feasible nor cost-effective.

questions.stem: For a large corporate issuer, the number of debt securities outstanding relative to the number of equity securities outstanding is most likely:

options.A: about the same.
options.B: smaller.
options.C: far larger.

rationales.A: The counts are not close. Large issuers commonly have dozens of bonds outstanding against one or two classes of equity: Royal Dutch Shell 57 fixed-income securities against 1 common equity, BHP Billiton 22 against 1, Johnson & Johnson 37 against 1, and Ford Motor Company 104 fixed-income securities against 2 common and 2 preferred. Those many near-substitute bonds are precisely what aids an enhanced index strategy.
rationales.B: The opposite holds. Issuers spread borrowing across many separate bonds rather than concentrating it in one or two: as of October 2020 Royal Dutch Shell had 57 bonds outstanding across four currencies, some both fixed and floating rate, with maturities from under a year out to 2052. A bond investor therefore faces many near substitutes for a single issuer, where an equity investor typically has one share class to choose from.
rationales.C: As of October 2020, Royal Dutch Shell had 57 bonds outstanding across four currencies, some of which were both fixed and floating rate, with a range of maturities from under a year to bonds maturing in 2052 — against a single class of common equity. Other large issuers look the same: BHP Billiton 22 fixed-income securities against 1 common equity, Johnson & Johnson 37 against 1, and Ford Motor Company 104 fixed-income securities against 2 classes of common equity and 2 of preferred. The existence of many debt securities for a particular issuer suggests that many near substitutes may exist for an investor seeking to pursue an enhanced index strategy.

questions.stem: Compared with equity markets, fixed-income markets most likely rely on:

options.A: quote-based execution through broker/dealers acting as principals.
options.B: order-based execution through central limit order books.
options.C: an execution process identical to that of equity markets.

rationales.A: Unlike equity securities, which trade primarily over an exchange, fixed-income markets are largely over-the-counter markets that rely on broker/dealers as principals to trade these securities using a quote-based execution process rather than the order-based trading systems common in equity markets. The rising cost of maintaining risk-weighted assets on dealer balance sheets because of Basel III capital requirements has had an adverse effect on fixed-income trading and liquidity: broker/dealers have reduced bond inventories because of higher capital costs. With lower trading inventories, dealers have a limited appetite to facilitate trading at narrow bid–offer spreads and are less willing to support larger block trades, preferring execution in smaller trade sizes. Finally, a significant decline in proprietary trading among dealers has had a greater pricing effect on less liquid, off-the-run bonds.
rationales.B: Bond markets are largely over-the-counter and quote-driven through broker/dealers acting as principals, not order-driven through exchange order books. Basel III capital requirements have raised the cost of carrying inventory on dealer balance sheets, so dealers hold fewer bonds, show less appetite for narrow bid–offer spreads and block trades, and price off-the-run issues less finely — frictions that depend on dealer capital rather than on a central limit order book.
rationales.C: The two structures differ in both venue and execution process: quote-based over-the-counter trading through dealer principals for bonds, against order-based exchange trading for equities. Bond liquidity consequently depends on dealer balance sheet capacity, and the average US investment-grade bond trade is far larger than the average stock trade.

questions.stem: Reporting of over-the-counter US corporate bond transactions is most likely:

options.A: voluntary, at each dealer's discretion.
options.B: mandatory under the TRACE system.
options.C: unavailable, as no such system exists.

rationales.A: Reporting is mandatory rather than discretionary: every broker/dealer that is a FINRA member firm must report an eligible corporate bond transaction within 15 minutes of its occurrence. Regulators built the TRACE system precisely because voluntary reporting left fixed-income trading difficult to track.
rationales.B: Fixed-income trading in many markets is difficult to track, so in some markets regulators developed systems that facilitate mandatory reporting of over-the-counter transactions in eligible fixed-income securities, such as the US Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine (TRACE). All broker/dealers that are Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) member firms must report corporate bond transactions within 15 minutes of occurrence. The distinct nature of fixed-income trading matters here: the vast majority of fixed-income securities either do not trade at all or trade only a few times during the year, and only a small fraction trade every business day. The average trade size in dollar terms in the US investment-grade bond market is also roughly 70 times the size of the average stock trade.
rationales.C: TRACE, the US Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine, is exactly such a system: a regulator-developed facility for mandatory reporting of over-the-counter transactions in eligible fixed-income securities, with FINRA member firms reporting corporate bond trades within 15 minutes.

questions.stem: Matrix pricing, also known as evaluated pricing, is best described as:

options.A: the use of a bond's last traded price, however stale.
options.B: the estimation of a price for a bond that is not actively traded.
options.C: the estimation of a price for an equity without a market quote.

rationales.A: Matrix pricing estimates a current market yield and price from observable liquid benchmark yields and the benchmark spreads of comparable bonds precisely because a stale last-trade price is unreliable for an instrument that rarely trades — and the vast majority of fixed-income securities either do not trade at all or trade only a few times a year.
rationales.B: The illiquid nature of most fixed-income instruments gives rise to pricing and valuation challenges for asset managers. For fixed-income instruments that are not actively traded and therefore do not have an observable price, it is common to use an estimation process known as matrix pricing, or evaluated pricing. Matrix pricing makes use of observable liquid benchmark yields, such as Treasuries of similar maturity and duration, as well as the benchmark spreads of bonds with comparable times to maturity, credit quality, and sector or security type, in order to estimate the current market yield and price. In practice, asset managers typically outsource this function to a global custodian or external vendor. This estimation analysis is another potential source of variation between index performance and portfolio returns.
rationales.C: Matrix pricing is a fixed-income estimation process, applied to bonds that are not actively traded rather than to equities; it works from Treasury benchmark yields and the spreads of comparable bonds, and asset managers typically outsource the function to a global custodian or external vendor.

questions.stem: Rebalancing of broad fixed-income market indexes most likely occurs:

options.A: monthly.
options.B: rarely.
options.C: semi-annually.

rationales.A: The complexity of trading and valuing individual fixed-income securities further underscores the challenges associated with managing an index-based bond portfolio. Fixed-income indexes change frequently as a result of both new debt issuance and the maturity of outstanding bonds, and bond index eligibility is also affected by changes in ratings and in bond callability. As a result, rebalancing of bond market indexes usually occurs monthly, rather than semi-annually or annually as it does for equity indexes. Fixed-income investors pursuing a pure indexing strategy therefore must also incur greater transaction costs associated with maintaining a bond portfolio consistent with the index.
rationales.B: Bond indexes do not sit still while their constituents run to maturity. New debt issuance adds securities, maturing bonds drop out, and changes in ratings and in callability alter eligibility, so the constituent list turns over continually and is rebalanced monthly.
rationales.C: This reverses the comparison. Semi-annual or annual rebalancing is the equity index convention; bond indexes rebalance more often, usually monthly, because new issuance, maturities, rating changes, and callability keep altering eligibility — and that higher turnover is why a pure bond indexing strategy carries greater transaction costs.

questions.stem: The primary risk factors a manager matches when indexing a bond portfolio most likely include:

options.A: portfolio modified adjusted duration.
options.B: portfolio Macaulay duration matched to the index's average maturity.
options.C: issuer equity beta, currency exposure, and dividend yield.

rationales.A: The primary indexing risk factors are six. (1) Portfolio modified adjusted duration: the duration measure must be option-adjusted so that the analysis reflects securities with embedded call risk, and larger rate moves should incorporate the second-order convexity adjustment. (2) Key rate duration: the effect of a rate change at a specific maturity along the yield curve while holding the remaining rates constant, which gauges the index's sensitivity to non-parallel yield curve shifts. (3) Percent in sector and quality: index yield is most effectively matched by targeting the same percentage weights across fixed-income sectors and credit quality. (4) Sector and quality spread duration contribution. (5) Sector, coupon and maturity call weights: managers should seek to match the coupon and maturity weights of callable bonds by sector. (6) Issuer exposure: concentration of issuers within a portfolio exposes the asset manager to issuer-specific event risk, so the manager should match the portfolio duration effect from holdings in each issuer. Modified adjusted duration is therefore the duration measure used, and it is the first of the six.
rationales.B: The duration factor is modified adjusted, that is option-adjusted, duration, not Macaulay duration matched to the index's average maturity. The option adjustment matters because index constituents carry embedded call risk, and for larger rate moves a convexity adjustment is added on top. Duration is also only the first of six factors: the others are key rate duration, percent in sector and quality, sector and quality spread duration contribution, sector/coupon/maturity call weights, and issuer exposure. Matching an average-maturity Macaulay figure would leave curve, spread, call and issuer exposures unmatched.
rationales.C: These are equity-style factors. The six fixed-income indexing risk factors are portfolio modified adjusted duration, key rate duration, percent in sector and quality, sector and quality spread duration contribution, sector/coupon/maturity call weights, and issuer exposure. Issuer equity beta, currency exposure and the dividend yield of the corporate sector play no part in matching a bond index's risk profile; the exposures that drive bond index tracking error are rate level, curve shape, spread, call risk and issuer concentration.

questions.stem: Spread duration is most likely:

options.A: not a recognized fixed-income risk measure.
options.B: the change in a non-Treasury bond's price for a change in its spread.
options.C: a Treasury bond's price sensitivity to its own benchmark yield.

rationales.A: Spread duration is the standard measure of price sensitivity to spread changes for non-Treasury securities, and matching it between the portfolio and the index is one of the primary indexing risk factors. The risk that a bond's price will change in response to an idiosyncratic rate move rather than an overall market yield change is known as spread risk, and spread duration is how that exposure is quantified.
rationales.B: For non-government fixed-income securities, the yield to maturity is separated into a benchmark yield, typically the most recently issued or on-the-run government bond with the closest time to maturity, and a spread reflecting the difference between the benchmark yield and the security-specific yield. The risk that a bond's price will change in response to an idiosyncratic rate move rather than an overall market yield change is spread risk. Spread duration measures that exposure: it refers to the change in a non-Treasury security's price given a widening or narrowing of the spread compared with the benchmark. Matching the relative quality between the portfolio and the fixed-income index will minimize this risk.
rationales.C: The concept applies to non-Treasury securities and isolates the spread component of yield rather than the benchmark component. A government bond's sensitivity to its own benchmark yield is captured by effective duration and key rate duration; spread duration captures the price change that comes from a widening or narrowing of the spread over that benchmark, which is why it is the risk factor matched by aligning the portfolio's credit quality with the index's.

questions.stem: The objective of the present value of distribution of cash flows methodology is most likely to match an index's:

options.A: overall Macaulay duration using a single representative bond.
options.B: yield curve risk across discrete cash flow vertices.
options.C: credit quality distribution across rating categories.

rationales.A: Matching one aggregate duration figure with a single representative bond leaves yield curve risk unaddressed: two portfolios with identical overall duration can respond very differently to a non-parallel shift. This methodology instead distributes present value across multiple semi-annual cash flow vertices and matches the index vertex by vertex, with each period's contribution to duration summing to the index's duration. The measure used is also modified adjusted duration rather than Macaulay duration matched to maturity.
rationales.B: This approach addresses a portfolio's sensitivity to rate changes along the yield curve by seeking to approximate and match the yield curve risk of an index over discrete time periods referred to as cash flow vertices. The steps are as follows. (1) The manager divides the cash flows for each non-callable security in the index into discrete semi-annual periods, aggregates them, and then adds the cash flows for callable securities in the index based on the probability of call for each given period. (2) The present value of the aggregated cash flows for each semi-annual period is computed, with the total present value of all such aggregated cash flows equal to the index's present value, and the percentage of the present value at each cash flow vertex is calculated. (3) Each time period is then multiplied by that vertex's proportionate share of the index. (4) Finally, each period's contribution to duration is added to arrive at a total representing the bond index's duration. Because the distribution of present value is matched vertex by vertex rather than only in aggregate, the portfolio's exposure to non-parallel curve shifts is matched as well.
rationales.C: Matching quality weights is the separate percent in sector and quality risk factor, under which index yield is matched by targeting the same percentage weights across fixed-income sectors and credit qualities. This methodology targets rate, or yield curve, risk across discrete time vertices by matching the proportion of the index's present value that falls in each semi-annual period.

questions.stem: Tracking error is most likely:

options.A: the standard deviation of a portfolio's active return over a period.
options.B: the maximum amount a portfolio's return can deviate from its benchmark.
options.C: the average difference between portfolio and benchmark returns.

rationales.A: Tracking error is the standard deviation of a portfolio's active return for a given period, where active return = portfolio return - benchmark index return. Minimizing it is the goal of matching the primary indexing risk factors. If returns are assumed to be normally distributed around the mean, then 68% of those returns will lie within one standard deviation of the mean. So if a fund's tracking error is 50 bps, then for approximately two-thirds of the time period observations the fund's return would be expected to be less than 50 bps above or below the index's return. On the same logic, a target tracking error of 1.25% means that, assuming normally distributed returns, in 68% or roughly two-thirds of time periods the fund should have a return within 1.25% of its benchmark index.
rationales.B: Tracking error is a one-standard-deviation dispersion measure, not a hard cap on deviation. Assuming normally distributed active returns, a tracking error of 1.25% says the portfolio's return falls within 1.25% of the index in roughly two-thirds of time periods; the remaining third of observations fall outside that band, and in principle the deviation in any single period is unbounded.
rationales.C: The mean active return is not tracking error, which is the standard deviation of active return. A portfolio could average an active return of zero and still show wide dispersion around that average, and it is exactly that dispersion, one standard deviation of which covers 68% of observations, that tracking error measures.

drills.los_text: compare alternative methods for establishing bond market exposure passively

questions.stem: Full replication of a bond index most likely:

options.A: is cost-effective for broad-based bond indexes.
options.B: requires rebalancing only annually.
options.C: requires holding thinly traded issues in exact index proportion.

rationales.A: Holding every constituent would minimize tracking error, but the cost of doing so is prohibitive. Sourcing a wide range of thinly traded securities in exact proportion, then rebalancing monthly as bonds roll down and new issues become eligible, generates a very significant number of purchases and sales. Although the large number of index constituents may well provide the best means of risk diversification, in practice full replication is neither feasible nor cost-effective for broad-based fixed-income indexes; it is impractical for all but the most narrow indexes, which is why enhanced indexing by stratified sampling is used instead.
rationales.B: Rolling bond maturities, as well as frequent new issuance eligible for inclusion in the index, drive a monthly rebalancing for most fixed-income indexes, not an annual one. That turnover, together with the sales forced when a security no longer meets index criteria because its maturity has shortened below one year or it has been downgraded below the average minimum investment-grade rating, is one of the main reasons full replication is impractical.
rationales.C: Initial index replication does not require manager analysis but rather involves sourcing a wide range of securities in exact proportion to the index, many of which may be thinly traded. The manager's ongoing task under full replication is to purchase or sell bonds when there are changes to the index, in addition to managing inflows and outflows for the fund. The manager may have to sell when a security no longer meets the index criteria, such as when it matures or is downgraded; for the Bloomberg Barclays US Aggregate Bond Index, a security becomes ineligible when it either has a maturity of less than one year or is downgraded below an average minimum investment-grade rating. On the other hand, managers must purchase newly issued securities that meet index criteria to maintain full replication, which, depending on the index, may occur quite frequently. Rolling maturities and frequent new issuance drive monthly rebalancing, and the number of purchases and sales required to maintain an exact proportional allocation is very significant for most bond indexes. As a result, full replication is neither feasible nor cost-effective for broad-based fixed-income indexes and is impractical for all but the most narrow indexes.

questions.stem: A stratified sampling approach to indexing a bond portfolio most likely:

options.A: holds every index security in its exact index proportion.
options.B: tracks the index closely while holding fewer securities.
options.C: matches the index's overall duration only.

rationales.A: Holding every security in its exact index proportion is full replication, the approach whose limitations stratified sampling exists to address. Stratified sampling instead identifies a subset of bonds or bond-linked exposures whose characteristics correspond to each cell: if an index contains 1,000 fixed-income securities of which 10% are AAA rated, the manager might choose only 5 to 10 AAA rated securities within that cell to mimic the performance of the index's AAA rated bonds. That is how the approach tracks the index while purchasing far fewer securities.
rationales.B: Many limitations of the full replication approach are addressed by an enhanced indexing strategy, whose goal is to mirror the most important index characteristics and still closely track index performance over time while purchasing fewer securities. This general approach is referred to as stratified sampling, or the cell approach, to indexing. First, each cell or significant index portfolio characteristic is identified and mapped to the current index. Second, the portfolio manager identifies a subset of bonds or bond-linked exposures, such as derivatives, with characteristics that correspond to the index. Finally, the positions in each cell are adjusted over time given changes to the underlying index versus existing portfolio positions. For example, if a fixed-income index contains 1,000 fixed-income securities, 10% of which are AAA rated, the portfolio manager might choose 5 to 10 AAA rated securities within that cell to mimic the performance of the AAA rated bonds within the index.
rationales.C: Cells are formed on the index's significant portfolio characteristics, which include sector and credit quality and not aggregate duration alone, and the positions in each cell are adjusted over time as the underlying index changes. Matching only overall duration would leave the sector, credit quality, spread duration and call exposures unmatched, and those are among the primary risk factors that drive tracking error.

questions.stem: Incorporating ESG factors into a bond index most likely involves:

options.A: overweighting green bond issues alone.
options.B: a business involvement screen and an ESG rating.
options.C: no identifiable components.

rationales.A: A green bond tilt is not the framework. The two components are an exclusionary business involvement screen and the integration of a third-party ESG rating, for instance a minimum MSCI rating requirement of BBB applied on top of the screen. Overweighting green issues is a separate portfolio decision and is neither of the two components.
rationales.B: There are two main components to incorporating ESG factors in an index. First, a business involvement screen excludes issuers involved in business lines or such activities as alcohol, gambling, tobacco, adult entertainment, nuclear power, and firearms. Second, an ESG rating, provided by one of numerous third-party companies, is applied. MSCI, one such company, provides ratings on an AAA to CCC scale using a rules-based methodology according to the companies' exposure to ESG risks and how well they are managed relative to peers. When building a sustainable index, for example, Bloomberg will apply such rules as those described and then further filter the constituents for business involvement and an MSCI minimum rating requirement of BBB. Given the proliferation of ESG data providers, there are differences across methodologies and ratings.
rationales.C: Two components are identified: a business involvement screen that excludes issuers involved in activities such as alcohol, gambling, tobacco, adult entertainment, nuclear power and firearms, and the application of a third-party ESG rating used to filter the remaining constituents, such as a minimum MSCI rating of BBB. What does vary across providers is the methodology and the resulting ratings, not the existence of the two components.

questions.stem: Enhancement strategies available to the manager of an indexed bond portfolio most likely include:

options.A: no such strategies.
options.B: lower-cost enhancements.
options.C: equity exposure enhancements.

rationales.A: Five categories of enhancement are catalogued: lower-cost enhancements, issue selection enhancements, yield curve enhancements, sector and quality enhancements, and call exposure enhancements. All of them are aimed at reducing the component of tracking error associated with the expenses and transaction costs of portfolio management, so the claim that no enhancement strategy is available is incorrect.
rationales.B: A number of enhancement strategies are available to portfolio managers seeking to reduce the component of tracking error associated with the expenses and transaction costs of portfolio management. (1) Lower-cost enhancements: minimizing fund expenses, or introducing a more competitive trading process to reduce the bid-offer cost of trading. (2) Issue selection enhancements: using bond valuation models to identify specific issues that are undervalued, or cheap, relative to their implied value. (3) Yield curve enhancements: using analytical models to gauge relative value across the term structure of interest rates. (4) Sector and quality enhancements: overweighting specific bond and credit sectors across the business cycle to enhance returns. (5) Call exposure enhancements: because effective duration is a sufficient risk measure only for relatively small rate changes, anticipated larger yield changes may affect bond performance significantly, especially when a bond shifts from trading to maturity to trading to an earlier call date. Callable securities priced on a yield-to-call basis and trading above par tend to be less price sensitive for a given effective duration than those priced on a yield-to-maturity basis, which suggests a manager should use metrics other than effective duration in that case when changing exposure.
rationales.C: The enhancements are fixed-income-native: lowering fund expenses and bid-offer trading costs, selecting cheap issues with bond valuation models, positioning across the term structure, overweighting bond and credit sectors across the business cycle, and managing call exposure. Adding equity exposure appears nowhere among them, and it would be an asset allocation decision rather than a way of recovering the tracking error that expenses and transaction costs create in an indexed bond portfolio.

questions.stem: Relative to bonds priced on a yield-to-maturity basis, callable bonds trading above par and priced on a yield-to-call basis are most likely:

options.A: equally price sensitive for a given effective duration.
options.B: more price sensitive for a given effective duration.
options.C: less price sensitive for a given effective duration.

rationales.A: The call feature does change the price sensitivity profile, which is why the pricing basis matters. Once an anticipated drop in yields moves a premium bond from being priced on a yield-to-maturity basis to being priced on a yield-to-call basis, further price appreciation is compressed, so two bonds with the same effective duration can respond quite differently to the same rate move. Effective duration is a sufficient risk measure only for relatively small rate changes for exactly this reason.
rationales.B: A premium callable priced on a yield-to-call basis tends to be less, not more, price sensitive for a given effective duration than a bond priced on a yield-to-maturity basis. The call caps the upside price response, so effective duration overstates the sensitivity, and the manager should use metrics other than effective duration when changing this exposure.
rationales.C: Because effective duration is a sufficient risk measure only for relatively small rate changes, anticipated larger yield changes may affect bond performance significantly, especially when a bond shifts from trading to maturity to trading to an earlier call date. For example, an anticipated drop in yields might cause a callable bond to shift from being priced on a yield-to-maturity basis to a yield-to-call basis. Callable fixed-income securities priced on a yield-to-call basis and trading above par tend to be less price sensitive for a given effective duration than those priced on a yield-to-maturity basis, because the call compresses further price appreciation. This suggests a manager should use metrics other than effective duration in this case when changing exposure.

questions.stem: Bond ETFs are most likely:

options.A: more liquid than mutual funds.
options.B: less liquid than the bonds they hold.
options.C: priced once per day at net asset value.

rationales.A: Several alternatives to direct investing in bonds are available to investment managers. Index-based exposure can be obtained through traded products such as ETFs, which offer greater liquidity than the underlying securities, or through other alternatives such as mutual funds, that is pooled investment vehicles whose shares or units represent a proportional share in the ownership of the assets in an underlying portfolio. Investors benefit from greater bond ETF liquidity versus mutual funds given the availability of ETF shares to be purchased or sold throughout the trading day. ETF authorized participants, who enter into an agreement with the distributor of the fund and purchase shares from or sell ETF shares to the fund in creation units, would be encouraged to engage in arbitrage to profit from any significant divergence between the market price of the underlying fixed-income securities portfolio and the ETF's net asset value. That said, the fact that many fixed-income securities are either thinly traded or not traded at all might allow such a divergence to persist.
rationales.B: ETFs typically offer greater liquidity than their underlying, often thinly traded, fixed-income constituents, and that is one of the main reasons managers use them to obtain index-based exposure. Authorized participant arbitrage links the ETF's market price to its net asset value, although thin trading or no trading in many of the underlying bonds can allow a divergence between the two to persist.
rationales.C: ETF shares trade continuously throughout the trading day, which is precisely the liquidity advantage they hold over mutual funds, whose units are priced once daily at net asset value. The intraday market price can diverge from net asset value, and authorized participants are encouraged to arbitrage any significant divergence.

questions.stem: A total return swap referencing a bond index is most likely:

options.A: An exchange-traded, centrally cleared contract.
options.B: An exchange of fixed cash flows for a floating-rate benchmark.
options.C: A common over-the-counter instrument.

rationales.A: A total return swap is a customized over-the-counter contract negotiated bilaterally between two counterparties, not an exchange-traded product settled through a central clearinghouse. That customization is in fact one of its attractions: it allows exposure to reference obligations that are difficult to access directly, such as some high-yield and commercial loan investments. It also means the receiver bears counterparty credit risk, which an exchange-traded, centrally cleared instrument would largely remove.
rationales.B: An exchange of a stream of fixed cash flows against a floating-rate benchmark such as the MRR describes a plain interest rate swap, which counterparties use to transform fixed assets or liabilities into variable exposure. A total return swap works differently: its periodic exchange is based on a reference obligation that is an underlying equity, commodity, or bond index. The total return receiver gets both the cash flows from the underlying index and any appreciation in the index over the period, in exchange for paying the MRR plus a pre-determined spread.
rationales.C: Index-based total return swaps are common over-the-counter instruments and an alternative to investing directly in fixed-income securities. Like an interest rate swap, a total return swap involves the periodic exchange of cash flows between two parties for the life of the contract. Unlike an interest rate swap, in which counterparties exchange a stream of fixed cash flows versus a floating-rate benchmark such as the MRR to transform fixed assets or liabilities to a variable exposure, a total return swap has a periodic exchange based on a reference obligation that is an underlying equity, commodity, or bond index. The total return receiver receives both the cash flows from the underlying index and any appreciation in the index over the period in exchange for paying the MRR plus a pre-determined spread. The total return payer is responsible for paying the reference obligation cash flows and return to the receiver but is also compensated by the receiver for any depreciation in the index or default losses incurred on the portfolio.

questions.stem: Relative to a direct investment in a bond portfolio, a total return swap most likely:

options.A: Eliminates counterparty credit risk.
options.B: Trades on an exchange without customization.
options.C: Requires less initial cash outlay.

rationales.A: A total return swap introduces counterparty credit risk rather than eliminating it. The total return receiver depends on the swap counterparty to pass through the reference obligation's cash flows and appreciation, so the receiver's economic outcome is contingent on that counterparty's performance in a way that outright ownership of the bonds is not. Direct ownership of a bond portfolio carries issuer credit risk, but it does not add a swap counterparty on top of it.
rationales.B: A total return swap is a customized over-the-counter product, not an exchange-traded one, and its customization is an advantage rather than a limitation: it can offer exposure to assets that are difficult to access directly, such as some high-yield and commercial loan investments. Daily exchange transparency and a standardized, non-customizable contract describe a listed future or an ETF, not a total return swap.
rationales.C: As a derivative, a total return swap requires less initial cash outlay than a direct investment in the bond portfolio for similar performance, which is its principal advantage over holding a bond mutual fund or ETF outright. The swap does carry counterparty credit risk, however. And as a customized over-the-counter product, a total return swap can offer exposure to assets that are difficult to access directly, such as some high-yield and commercial loan investments.

questions.stem: Paisley buys and holds a bond index with half its weight in short-term bank bills; Dundee matches the duration of a composite benchmark and seeks to add value through an enhanced indexing approach; Newcastleton is actively managed with a mandate to take duration and credit positions that deviate from its index. The lowest-risk fund of the three is most likely:

options.A: Dundee.
options.B: Newcastleton.
options.C: Paisley.

rationales.A: Dundee represents a medium risk profile, not the lowest of the three. Its composite benchmark and enhanced indexing approach mean it matches index duration while adding value through fundamental strategies, which places it in the middle of the risk spectrum. It would be the best choice for a middle-aged worker seeking to add a fixed-income component with moderate risk, rather than for an investor seeking minimum risk.
rationales.B: Newcastleton has the highest risk of the three, not the lowest. It is an actively managed fund with a mandate to take positions in primary risk factors such as duration and credit that deviate from those of the index in order to generate excess return. That makes it an appropriate choice for a younger worker who wants fixed-income exposure and is willing to accommodate higher risk.
rationales.C: Paisley represents the lowest risk of the three choices, given both its choice of underlying bond index, half of which sits in short-term securities tracking a bank bill index, and its lack of active management strategies under a buy-and-hold approach. It is a suitable choice for an investor near retirement who is seeking income with a minimum risk profile. By comparison, Dundee carries a medium risk profile, given its composite benchmark and enhanced indexing approach, matching index duration while adding value through fundamental strategies, and suits a middle-aged worker; Newcastleton carries the highest risk, as an actively managed fund with a mandate to take duration and credit positions that deviate from the index, and suits a younger worker.

questions.stem: Australian superannuation plans are most likely:

options.A: Government-supported retirement savings arrangements.
options.B: Government-guaranteed defined benefit pension plans.
options.C: Voluntary schemes with no employer contribution mandate.

rationales.A: Superannuation funds are Australian government-supported arrangements for Australian workers to save for retirement. They combine a government-mandated minimum percentage of wages contributed by employers with a voluntary employee contribution that offers tax benefits, and they are similar in structure to the defined contribution plans common in the United States, Europe, and Asia. A superannuation fund such as Adelaide Super typically offers its members a range of fixed-interest investment choices.
rationales.B: Superannuation plans are similar to the defined contribution plans common in the United States, Europe, and Asia: the member's retirement outcome depends on contributions made and the investment returns earned on the member's chosen options, which is why members are offered a range of fixed-interest and other investment choices. The government mandates a minimum employer contribution percentage and supports the arrangement through tax benefits, but it does not guarantee a defined benefit.
rationales.C: Superannuation is not purely voluntary. It combines a government-mandated minimum percentage of wages contributed by employers with a voluntary employee contribution that offers tax benefits. The mandated employer component is what distinguishes it from a discretionary savings scheme; the voluntary member contribution sits on top of that floor.

questions.stem: An investor who chooses full index replication over an active bond mandate is most likely expressing the expectation that:

options.A: a skilled active manager can be identified in advance.
options.B: replication outperforms skilled managers gross of fees.
options.C: active managers cannot consistently outperform on a risk-adjusted basis.

rationales.A: This reverses the reasoning behind replication. Index replication is chosen in part because the investor cannot identify a skilled manager in advance, or is not prepared to go through the periods of underperformance that an active mandate involves. An investor confident of identifying skill ex ante would hire the manager rather than replicate. Initial index replication does not require manager analysis at all; it involves sourcing a wide range of securities in exact proportion to the index, many of which may be thinly traded.
rationales.B: The case for replication is not that it beats skilled managers before fees. It rests on the expectation that an active manager cannot consistently outperform the index on a risk-adjusted basis, that the investor cannot identify a skilled manager in advance, or that the investor is not prepared to go through periods of underperformance. Replication aims to deliver the index return, not to exceed what a skilled manager could earn gross of fees.
rationales.C: Index replication is done based on the expectation that (i) an active manager cannot consistently outperform the index on a risk-adjusted basis, (ii) the investor cannot identify a skilled manager in advance, or (iii) the investor is not prepared to go through periods of underperformance. Initial index replication does not require manager analysis but rather involves sourcing a wide range of securities in exact proportion to the index, many of which may be thinly traded. In practice, investors who wish to have exposure to an index often rely on one of the many ETFs that exist in this space rather than replicating the index security by security.

drills.los_text: discuss criteria for selecting a benchmark and justify the selection of a benchmark

questions.stem: The choice of a fixed-income benchmark is most likely:

options.A: Relevant only to active mandates.
options.B: The first step of the asset allocation process.
options.C: A manager's most important decision beyond passive versus active.

rationales.A: The benchmark defines what a passive portfolio holds, so the choice matters at least as much for a passive mandate as for an active one: it sets the duration profile, the issuer mix, and the risk and return characteristics the investor will actually own. The choice of a benchmark is perhaps an investment manager's most important decision beyond the passive versus active decision or the form that the investment takes.
rationales.B: Benchmark selection is one of the final steps in the broader asset allocation process, not the first. That process starts with a clear delineation of the portfolio manager's investment goals and objectives; the benchmark is chosen once those goals, and the duration and risk and return preferences that follow from them, are clear.
rationales.C: The choice of a benchmark is perhaps an investment manager's most important decision beyond the passive versus active decision or the form that the investment takes. Benchmark selection is one of the final steps in the broader asset allocation process, which starts with a clear delineation of the portfolio manager's investment goals and objectives. Because the benchmark embeds a duration profile and an issuer and sector mix, it determines most of the portfolio's systematic exposure whether the mandate is run passively or actively.

questions.stem: Widely accepted use of an index as a fixed-income benchmark most likely requires:

options.A: No criteria beyond publication of the index.
options.B: Transparent inclusion rules, investability, and daily valuation.
options.C: A minimum number of constituent securities.

rationales.A: Publication alone is not sufficient. Benchmark selection must factor in the broad range of issuers and characteristics available in the fixed-income markets, and in general the use of an index as a widely accepted benchmark requires clear, transparent rules for security inclusion and weighting, investability, daily valuation and availability of past returns, and turnover. An index that fails those tests cannot be tracked or evaluated reliably, however widely it is quoted.
rationales.B: Benchmark selection must factor in the broad range of issuers and characteristics available in the fixed-income markets. In general, the use of an index as a widely accepted benchmark requires clear, transparent rules for security inclusion and weighting, investability, daily valuation and availability of past returns, and turnover. Clear rules let an investor know what the index will hold; investability means the constituents can actually be bought in the weights specified; daily valuation and a return history make tracking error and performance measurable; and turnover indicates how much trading tracking the index will demand.
rationales.C: There is no security-count threshold among the benchmark criteria. What is required is clear, transparent rules for security inclusion and weighting, investability, daily valuation and availability of past returns, and turnover. A narrow index meeting those tests can serve as a benchmark, while a very broad one that is not investable or not valued daily cannot.

questions.stem: Unlike an equity benchmark, a broad fixed-income benchmark most likely exhibits:

options.A: Upward duration drift in a static portfolio.
options.B: Downward duration drift in a static portfolio.
options.C: Stable issuer composition across market cycles.

rationales.A: Duration drifts in the opposite direction. Bonds have finite maturities, so in a static portfolio each holding moves closer to maturity with the passage of time and its duration falls; the portfolio's duration therefore drifts downward, not upward, unless the manager reinvests into longer maturities. This is one of the reasons fixed-income market dynamics drive deviation from the stable benchmark exposure investors seek, a problem equity indexes do not have.
rationales.B: Fixed-income market dynamics can drive deviation from a stable benchmark for two reasons. First, the finite maturity of bonds in a static portfolio implies that duration will drift downward over time as each holding ages toward maturity. Second, market dynamics and issuer preferences tend to dictate both the issuer composition of broad-based indexes and the maturity selection of narrower indexes: the composition of the Bloomberg Barclays US Aggregate Bond Index, for instance, changed significantly in the years before and after the 2008 global financial crisis, with a large increase in securitized debt pre-crisis and a significant rise in government debt thereafter.
rationales.C: Issuer composition is not stable. Market dynamics and issuer preferences tend to dictate both the issuer composition of broad-based indexes and the maturity selection of narrower indexes, because an index holds whatever issuers choose to bring to market. The Bloomberg Barclays US Aggregate Bond Index illustrates the point: securitized debt rose sharply before the 2008 global financial crisis, and government debt rose significantly afterward.

questions.stem: A broad US aggregate bond index reported sector weights of 53.0% government, 17.0% corporate, and 30.0% securitized in 1993; 38.0%, 24.0%, and 39.0% in 2000; 38.6%, 17.7%, and 43.7% in 2008; 45.8%, 18.8%, and 35.5% in 2010; and 43.4%, 27.3%, and 29.3% in 2020. The index's sector composition over this period is most likely characterized by:

options.A: A stable sector mix throughout the period.
options.B: A one-directional decline in the government weight.
options.C: A rising securitized share, then a government rebound.

rationales.A: The mix shifted materially rather than holding steady. Government fell from 53.0% in 1993 to 38.0% by 2000 and 38.6% by 2008 before rebounding to 45.8% in 2010 and standing at 43.4% in 2020; securitized rose from 30.0% to 39.0% and then to a peak of 43.7% in 2008 before falling back to 29.3% in 2020; corporate moved from 17.0% to 27.3%. Swings of 10 to 15 percentage points in a sector weight are not a stable mix, and they are the reason a fixed-income benchmark is a moving target in a way an equity index is not.
rationales.B: The government weight did fall through the 1990s and 2000s, from 53.0% in 1993 to 38.0% in 2000 and 38.6% in 2008, but it then rose again to 45.8% in 2010 and remained elevated at 43.4% in 2020 as post-crisis Treasury issuance surged. The path is not one-directional, and corporate debt did not displace Treasuries in every period: the corporate weight itself fell from 24.0% in 2000 to 17.7% in 2008 before climbing to 27.3% by 2020.
rationales.C: The securitized share rose from 30.0% in 1993 to 39.0% in 2000 and peaked at 43.7% in 2008 as pre-crisis securitized issuance expanded, then fell back to 35.5% in 2010 and 29.3% in 2020. The government share moved the other way, falling from 53.0% in 1993 to 38.0% in 2000 and 38.6% in 2008 before rebounding to 45.8% in 2010 and 43.4% in 2020 on heavy post-crisis Treasury issuance. Corporate debt grew over the full period from 17.0% to 27.3%. The episode shows how market dynamics and issuer preferences, rather than the investor's own preferences, dictate the issuer composition of a broad-based bond index.

questions.stem: The role played by beta in an equity portfolio is most likely played in a fixed-income portfolio by:

options.A: credit rating.
options.B: targeted duration.
options.C: no comparable measure.

rationales.A: Credit quality is a risk factor a fixed-income investor chooses, but it is not the portfolio's systematic exposure in the sense beta captures. The dynamics of fixed-income markets require investors to define their underlying duration preferences and a desired risk and return profile when conducting benchmark selection, and it is the desired duration profile, not the rating, that plays the beta role. Credit exposure is better thought of as one of the sub-benchmark choices layered on top of that duration decision.
rationales.B: The desired duration profile may be considered the portfolio 'beta,' with the targeted duration equal to an investor's preferred duration exposure. The dynamics of fixed-income markets require investors to more actively understand and define their underlying duration preferences, as well as a desired risk and return profile within their fixed-income allocation, when conducting benchmark selection. Once these parameters are clear, investors may wish to combine several well-defined sub-benchmark categories into an overall benchmark; examples include Treasuries or other domestic sovereign bonds, US agencies or other asset-backed securities, corporate bonds, high-yield bonds, bank loans, developed markets global debt, and emerging markets debt.
rationales.C: Fixed income does have an analog. The desired duration profile may be considered the portfolio 'beta,' with the targeted duration equal to the investor's preferred duration exposure, and it is set during benchmark selection along with the desired risk and return profile. Once that is fixed, the investor can combine well-defined sub-benchmark categories, such as sovereigns, agencies and asset-backed securities, corporates, high yield, bank loans, developed markets global debt, and emerging markets debt, into an overall benchmark.

questions.stem: Smart beta in fixed income is most likely to:

options.A: use simple, transparent, rules-based strategies.
options.B: be unavailable outside equity portfolios.
options.C: use discretionary active strategies at full active fees.

rationales.A: Smart beta involves the use of simple, transparent, rules-based strategies as a basis for investment decisions. For investors seeking to combine the potential outperformance of active management with a broad exposure to an index, a smart beta approach might be suitable. The starting point for smart beta investors is an analysis of the well-established, static strategies that tend to drive excess portfolio returns. In theory, asset managers who can isolate and pursue such strategies can capture a significant proportion of these excess returns without the significantly higher fees associated with active management. Use of smart beta strategies is more established among equity managers, but fixed-income managers are increasing their use of these techniques as well.
rationales.B: Smart beta is not confined to equities. Although its use is more established among equity managers, fixed-income managers are increasing their use of the same rules-based techniques.
rationales.C: Smart beta is rules-based rather than discretionary. It isolates and pursues well-established, static drivers of excess return through simple, transparent rules, which is precisely how it captures much of that excess return without the significantly higher fees associated with discretionary active management.

questions.stem: When choosing a fixed-income benchmark, an investor's implicit or explicit duration preferences are most likely:

options.A: a minor stylistic factor with no structural basis.
options.B: of no relevance to the decision.
options.C: a key consideration, given embedded asset/liability exposure.

rationales.A: The preference is structural, not stylistic. Fixed-income exposure already embedded in the investor's asset/liability portfolio determines which benchmark duration is appropriate, so the duration preference has a concrete balance-sheet grounding.
rationales.B: Embedded asset/liability duration exposure makes the investor's implicit or explicit duration preference central to the benchmark choice rather than irrelevant to it; the manager cannot select a benchmark without regard to it.
rationales.C: Choosing a fixed-income benchmark is unique in that the investor usually has some degree of fixed-income exposure embedded within its asset/liability portfolio, as in immunization and liability-driven investing. The investment manager must therefore consider these implicit or explicit duration preferences when choosing a fixed-income benchmark.

questions.stem: A highly risk-averse investor who is sensitive to fluctuations in portfolio value is most likely to prefer a bond index with:

options.A: short or intermediate duration and limited credit risk.
options.B: any duration, since risk aversion is not a factor.
options.C: the longest duration available.

rationales.A: Given a high degree of risk aversion and sensitivity to fluctuations in portfolio value, an index with short or intermediate duration and limited credit risk is most appropriate because it limits market value risk. Among typical alternatives, the S&P Eurozone Sovereign Bond 1-3 Years Index or the FTSE 1-3 Years Pfandbrief Index, given the high credit quality of covered bonds, would be appropriate choices.
rationales.B: Risk aversion drives the recommendation directly: a high degree of risk aversion is what calls for limited duration and high credit quality, so it is the governing factor in the choice rather than an irrelevant one.
rationales.C: Sensitivity to fluctuations in portfolio value points to short or intermediate duration. The longest-duration index available would maximize market value risk, which is the opposite of what this investor wants.

questions.stem: Pfandbriefs are most likely:

options.A: the largest segment of the German private debt market.
options.B: high-yield securities issued by German industrial corporations.
options.C: unsecured senior notes issued by the German federal government.

rationales.A: The Pfandbrief represents the largest segment of the German private debt market. It is a bond issued by German mortgage banks, collateralized by long-term assets such as real estate or public sector loans. These securities are also referred to as covered bonds and are being used as a model for similar issuance in other European countries. FTSE Pfandbrief indexes include jumbo Pfandbriefs from German issuers as well as those of comparable structure and quality from other Eurozone countries.
rationales.B: Pfandbriefs are high-credit-quality covered bonds issued by German mortgage banks and collateralized by real estate or public sector loans. They are not high-yield debt of industrial corporations.
rationales.C: Pfandbriefs are collateralized covered bonds issued by German mortgage banks, backed by long-term assets such as real estate or public sector loans. They are neither unsecured nor obligations of the German federal government.

questions.stem: The asset allocation process is most likely to:

options.A: begin with a clear delineation of investment goals and objectives.
options.B: follow from the benchmark, which determines the objectives.
options.C: proceed without a structured link between objectives and benchmark.

rationales.A: The asset allocation process starts with a clear delineation of the portfolio manager's investment goals and objectives. Examples of such goals include protection of funds, especially against inflation, broad market replication, predictable returns within acceptable risk parameters, or maximum absolute returns through opportunistic means. The manager must agree on an investment policy with the asset owners, beneficiaries, and other constituents, outlining return objectives, risk tolerance, and constraints in order to narrow the choices available in the broader capital markets to meet those objectives. A strategic asset allocation targeting specific weightings for each permissible asset class is the result of this process, while a tactical asset allocation range often provides the investment manager some short-term flexibility to deviate from those weightings in response to anticipated market changes.
rationales.B: The sequence runs the other way. Goals and objectives are delineated first and are set out in an agreed investment policy; the strategic asset allocation and the benchmark then follow from them, so the benchmark cannot determine the objectives.
rationales.C: The process is structured. Stated objectives such as inflation protection, broad market replication, predictable returns within acceptable risk parameters, or maximum absolute returns drive the investment policy, the strategic asset allocation, and in turn the benchmark decision.
